Name: Life Insurance
Plain-English Description: Pays money to chosen people (beneficiaries) when the insured person dies, and some types also build cash value you can use while alive.
Example: A parent buys a policy so their family can pay off the mortgage and college costs if the parent dies.
US Notes: Regulated by states; policy forms filed with each state insurance department. State guaranty associations protect policyholders if an insurer fails (typically at least $300,000 death benefit).
Full Path: Life Insurance

Name: Term Life
Plain-English Description: Covers you only for a fixed period, such as 10, 20 or 30 years, and pays out only if you die within that period. It has no cash value, which makes it the cheapest life cover.
Example: A 30-year-old buys a 30-year term policy that matches the length of their mortgage.
US Notes: The most common individual life product sold in the US by policy count.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Term Life

Name: Level Term
Plain-English Description: The death benefit and premium stay the same for the whole term (e.g. 10, 15, 20 or 30 years).
Example: A family buys $500,000 of cover that stays at $500,000 for 20 years.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Term Life > Level Term

Name: Decreasing Term
Plain-English Description: The death benefit shrinks over time, usually in line with a mortgage balance.
Example: A couple buys cover that falls each year as their mortgage is paid down.
US Notes: Often marketed by mortgage servicers via direct mail.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Term Life > Decreasing Term

Name: Annually Renewable Term (ART)
Plain-English Description: One-year cover that can be renewed each year without a new medical exam, with the premium rising as you age.
Example: A person needs cover for a short, uncertain period and renews year by year.
US Notes: YRT is also the most common basis for life reinsurance.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Term Life > Annually Renewable Term (ART)

Name: Convertible Term
Plain-English Description: Term cover that can be switched into a permanent policy later without new medical questions.
Example: Someone buys cheap term cover now, planning to convert to whole life when their income grows.
US Notes: Most US level term policies include a conversion privilege up to a set age.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Term Life > Convertible Term

Name: Return of Premium Term (ROP)
Plain-English Description: Term cover that refunds the premiums you paid if you are still alive at the end of the term. It costs more than plain term.
Example: A buyer who dislikes "wasting" premiums picks a policy that returns them at the end of 30 years.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Term Life > Return of Premium Term (ROP)

Name: Credit Life Insurance
Plain-English Description: Pays off a specific loan if the borrower dies; often offered by the lender at the time of the loan.
Example: A car buyer is offered a policy that clears the auto loan if the buyer dies.
US Notes: Rates and sales practices are tightly regulated by states; must be optional for the borrower.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Term Life > Credit Life Insurance

Name: Permanent Life
Plain-English Description: Covers you for your whole life as long as premiums are paid, and most types build a cash value you can borrow against or withdraw.
Example: A business owner buys permanent cover to leave money to heirs regardless of when they die.
US Notes: Cash value grows tax-deferred if the policy meets the IRC Section 7702 definition of life insurance; overfunded policies become Modified Endowment Contracts (MECs).
Full Path: Life Insurance > Permanent Life

Name: Whole Life
Plain-English Description: Lifelong cover with fixed premiums, a guaranteed death benefit and a guaranteed cash value that grows slowly.
Example: A grandparent buys a whole life policy to leave a guaranteed sum to grandchildren.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Permanent Life > Whole Life

Name: Participating Whole Life
Also Known As: Par whole life; Dividend-paying whole life
Plain-English Description: Whole life that may pay yearly dividends from the insurer's surplus, which can buy paid-up additions, reduce premiums or be taken as cash.
Example: A policyholder uses dividends from a mutual insurer to buy paid-up additions.
US Notes: Sold mainly by mutual insurers (e.g. Northwestern Mutual, MassMutual, New York Life). Dividends are not guaranteed.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Permanent Life > Whole Life > Participating Whole Life

Name: Non-Participating Whole Life
Plain-English Description: Whole life with fixed guarantees and no dividends, usually at a lower premium.
Example: A buyer wants predictable costs without dividends.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Permanent Life > Whole Life > Non-Participating Whole Life

Name: Limited Pay Whole Life
Plain-English Description: Whole life where premiums are paid for a set number of years or until a certain age, but cover lasts for life.
Example: A 40-year-old pays for 20 years so nothing is owed in retirement.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Permanent Life > Whole Life > Limited Pay Whole Life

Name: Single Premium Whole Life (SPWL)
Plain-English Description: Whole life bought with one lump-sum payment.
Example: A retiree moves an inheritance into a single-premium policy for their heirs.
US Notes: Usually a Modified Endowment Contract (MEC), so loans and withdrawals are taxed less favorably.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Permanent Life > Whole Life > Single Premium Whole Life (SPWL)

Name: Final Expense Insurance
Plain-English Description: Small whole life policy (often $5,000-$25,000), with simplified medical questions, meant to cover funeral and end-of-life costs.
Example: A 70-year-old buys $10,000 of cover so their children won't have to pay for the funeral.
US Notes: Heavily marketed to seniors aged 50-85.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Permanent Life > Whole Life > Final Expense Insurance

Name: Guaranteed Issue Whole Life
Plain-English Description: Whole life that accepts anyone in the eligible age range with no health questions; benefits are usually limited in the first two years (a "graded" death benefit).
Example: A person with serious health conditions who can't qualify elsewhere buys a small guaranteed policy.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Permanent Life > Whole Life > Guaranteed Issue Whole Life

Name: Industrial / Home Service Life
Plain-English Description: Very small whole life policies historically sold door to door with weekly or monthly premium collection.
Example: A family in the 1950s paid a collector each week for a small burial policy.
US Notes: Largely a legacy product; few new sales today.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Permanent Life > Whole Life > Industrial / Home Service Life

Name: Universal Life (UL)
Plain-English Description: Permanent cover with flexible premiums and an adjustable death benefit; the cash value earns interest credited in different ways depending on the type.
Example: A self-employed person with uneven income varies their payments each year.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Permanent Life > Universal Life (UL)

Name: Current Assumption Universal Life
Plain-English Description: The cash value earns an interest rate declared by the insurer, with a minimum guaranteed rate.
Example: A buyer wants flexible permanent cover with steady, insurer-declared interest.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Permanent Life > Universal Life (UL) > Current Assumption Universal Life

Name: Guaranteed Universal Life (GUL)
Plain-English Description: UL built mainly for a guaranteed lifelong death benefit at the lowest cost, with little cash value.
Example: A retiree wants guaranteed cover to age 100+ for estate planning at a lower price than whole life.
US Notes: Popular for estate planning. Reserves for older policies follow NAIC Actuarial Guideline 38 (AXXX); policies issued from 2020 use principles-based reserving (VM-20).
Full Path: Life Insurance > Permanent Life > Universal Life (UL) > Guaranteed Universal Life (GUL)

Name: Indexed Universal Life (IUL)
Plain-English Description: Cash value earns interest linked to a stock market index (e.g. the S&P 500), subject to a cap and a floor (often 0%). The floor stops index losses, but policy charges and cost of insurance can still reduce the cash value.
Example: A buyer wants some market-linked growth in their policy without direct stock market losses.
US Notes: Illustrations are regulated by NAIC Actuarial Guideline 49-A. Not a registered security.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Permanent Life > Universal Life (UL) > Indexed Universal Life (IUL)

Name: Variable Universal Life (VUL)
Plain-English Description: Cash value is invested in sub-accounts similar to mutual funds, so it can grow or lose value.
Example: An investor comfortable with risk picks equity funds inside their life policy.
US Notes: Regulated as a security: sold with a prospectus by FINRA-registered representatives.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Permanent Life > Universal Life (UL) > Variable Universal Life (VUL)

Name: Survivorship Universal Life
Plain-English Description: Covers two people (usually spouses) and pays out only after both have died.
Example: A wealthy couple buys cover to pay estate taxes their heirs will owe after both die.
US Notes: Often owned by an Irrevocable Life Insurance Trust (ILIT) to keep proceeds out of the taxable estate.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Permanent Life > Universal Life (UL) > Survivorship Universal Life

Name: Variable Life
Plain-English Description: Permanent cover with fixed premiums where the cash value and possibly the death benefit depend on investment performance.
Example: A policyholder chooses investment sub-accounts inside a fixed-premium policy.
US Notes: Regulated as a security (SEC/FINRA) as well as by state insurance departments.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Permanent Life > Variable Life

Name: Annuities
Plain-English Description: Turns a lump sum or series of payments into a stream of income, often for life. Annuities protect against outliving your savings rather than dying early.
Example: A retiree uses part of their savings to buy guaranteed monthly income for life.
US Notes: Sold by life insurers; earnings grow tax-deferred. Fixed annuities are state-regulated; variable and registered index-linked annuities are also SEC/FINRA-regulated.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Annuities

Name: Immediate Annuity
Also Known As: Single Premium Immediate Annuity (SPIA); Income annuity
Plain-English Description: A lump sum is paid in and income starts right away, usually within a year.
Example: A 67-year-old pays $200,000 and receives about $1,200 a month for life.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Annuities > Immediate Annuity

Name: Deferred Annuity
Plain-English Description: Money grows for years before income starts.
Example: A 50-year-old invests now to start income at 65.
US Notes: Withdrawals before age 59 1/2 usually face a 10% IRS penalty on earnings.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Annuities > Deferred Annuity

Name: Fixed Annuity
Plain-English Description: Earns a guaranteed fixed interest rate for a set period.
Example: A cautious saver locks in a 5% rate for 5 years.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Annuities > Deferred Annuity > Fixed Annuity

Name: Fixed Indexed Annuity (FIA)
Plain-English Description: Interest is linked to a market index with a cap and a zero floor, so principal isn't lost to market drops (though surrender charges and rider fees can reduce what you get back if you withdraw early).
Example: A pre-retiree wants some index-linked growth with no loss of principal.
US Notes: State-regulated insurance product, not a security.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Annuities > Deferred Annuity > Fixed Indexed Annuity (FIA)

Name: Variable Annuity
Plain-English Description: Money is invested in sub-accounts, so value can rise or fall; optional riders can guarantee income or a death benefit.
Example: An investor holds funds inside a variable annuity with a lifetime income rider.
US Notes: Sold with a prospectus; FINRA Rule 2330 governs suitability.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Annuities > Deferred Annuity > Variable Annuity

Name: Guaranteed Minimum Death Benefit (GMDB)
Plain-English Description: A variable annuity rider guaranteeing heirs receive at least a set amount (e.g. premiums paid or a high-water mark) even if investments fell.
Example: Markets drop 30% but the owner's heirs still get the full amount invested.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Annuities > Deferred Annuity > Variable Annuity > Guaranteed Minimum Death Benefit (GMDB)

Name: Guaranteed Lifetime Withdrawal Benefit (GLWB)
Plain-English Description: A rider that lets you withdraw a set percentage each year for life, even if the account value runs out.
Example: A retiree withdraws 5% of a $400,000 benefit base every year for life.
US Notes: The most common living benefit rider on US variable and indexed annuities.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Annuities > Deferred Annuity > Variable Annuity > Guaranteed Lifetime Withdrawal Benefit (GLWB)

Name: Guaranteed Minimum Income Benefit (GMIB)
Plain-English Description: A rider guaranteeing a minimum level of lifetime income if the contract is annuitized after a waiting period.
Example: An owner annuitizes at 70 using a guaranteed income base.
US Notes: Less widely sold today than GLWBs.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Annuities > Deferred Annuity > Variable Annuity > Guaranteed Minimum Income Benefit (GMIB)

Name: Guaranteed Minimum Accumulation Benefit (GMAB)
Plain-English Description: A rider guaranteeing the account will be worth at least a set amount after a waiting period, such as 10 years.
Example: After 10 years the account is topped up to the original premium.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Annuities > Deferred Annuity > Variable Annuity > Guaranteed Minimum Accumulation Benefit (GMAB)

Name: Registered Index-Linked Annuity (RILA)
Plain-English Description: Index-linked returns with a buffer or floor that limits (but does not remove) losses, in exchange for higher caps.
Example: A saver accepts losses beyond -10% in exchange for a higher upside cap.
US Notes: SEC-registered; one of the fastest-growing US annuity categories since 2020.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Annuities > Deferred Annuity > Registered Index-Linked Annuity (RILA)

Name: Qualifying Longevity Annuity Contract (QLAC)
Plain-English Description: A deferred annuity bought with retirement account (e.g. IRA, 401(k)) money that can start paying as late as age 85.
Example: A retiree uses part of an IRA to guarantee income from age 85.
US Notes: Premium limit set by IRS and indexed for inflation ($210,000 for 2025 and 2026, up from $200,000 set by SECURE 2.0). Excluded from required minimum distributions until payments start.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Annuities > Deferred Annuity > Qualifying Longevity Annuity Contract (QLAC)

Name: Joint and Survivor Annuity
Plain-English Description: Keeps paying income while either of two people is alive, sometimes at a reduced rate after the first dies.
Example: A married couple buys an annuity that pays until the second spouse dies.
US Notes: ERISA requires this as the default form for married participants in many pension plans.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Annuities > Joint and Survivor Annuity

Name: Structured Settlement Annuity
Plain-English Description: An annuity used to pay a lawsuit or injury settlement as a stream of payments instead of a lump sum.
Example: An injury victim receives monthly payments for 30 years from a settlement.
US Notes: Payments for physical injury are generally tax-free under IRC Section 104.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Annuities > Structured Settlement Annuity

Name: Pension Risk Transfer (Group Annuity)
Plain-English Description: An employer pays an insurer to take over its pension obligations, and the insurer pays retirees' pensions.
Example: A manufacturer transfers its retirees' pensions to a life insurer.
US Notes: Governed by ERISA and Department of Labor Interpretive Bulletin 95-1 on selecting annuity providers.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Annuities > Pension Risk Transfer (Group Annuity)

Name: Group & Business Life Insurance
Plain-English Description: Life and related covers bought by an employer for staff as part of a benefits package.
Example: A tech company offers life cover, disability cover and a retirement plan to all employees.
US Notes: Most employer benefit plans are governed by ERISA.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Group & Business Life Insurance

Name: Group Term Life
Plain-English Description: Employer-paid life cover, usually a flat amount or a multiple of salary, lasting while the person is employed.
Example: An employee's family receives 2x salary if they die while employed.
US Notes: Employer-paid coverage above $50,000 creates taxable imputed income for the employee (IRC Section 79).
Full Path: Life Insurance > Group & Business Life Insurance > Group Term Life

Name: Supplemental / Voluntary Life
Plain-English Description: Extra life cover that employees can buy through work at group rates, paid via payroll.
Example: An employee adds $300,000 of extra cover beyond the free employer-paid amount.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Group & Business Life Insurance > Supplemental / Voluntary Life

Name: Dependent Life
Plain-English Description: Small group life coverage on an employee's spouse and children.
Example: An employee adds $20,000 of cover for their spouse.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Group & Business Life Insurance > Dependent Life

Name: Key Person Insurance
Plain-English Description: A business insures the life of a vital employee or owner, and the business receives the payout.
Example: A startup insures its founder CTO so it can afford to replace her if she dies.
US Notes: Employer-owned policies must meet IRC Section 101(j) notice and consent rules for tax-free proceeds.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Group & Business Life Insurance > Key Person Insurance

Name: Buy-Sell Funding
Plain-English Description: Life cover used to fund an agreement where surviving owners buy a deceased owner's share of the business.
Example: Two partners each insure the other so the survivor can buy out the family of the deceased.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Group & Business Life Insurance > Buy-Sell Funding

Name: Corporate-Owned Life Insurance (COLI)
Plain-English Description: Life policies owned by a company on employees, often used to fund executive benefit obligations.
Example: A bank owns policies on executives to help fund deferred compensation.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Group & Business Life Insurance > Corporate-Owned Life Insurance (COLI)

Name: Split-Dollar Life
Plain-English Description: An arrangement where an employer and employee share the cost and benefits of a permanent life policy.
Example: A company pays premiums on an executive's policy and recovers them at death.
US Notes: Taxed under IRS split-dollar regulations (2003).
Full Path: Life Insurance > Group & Business Life Insurance > Split-Dollar Life

Name: Life Insurance Riders
Plain-English Description: Optional extras added to a life policy, often for an extra premium.
Example: A buyer adds a waiver of premium rider to a term policy.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Life Insurance Riders

Name: Accidental Death Benefit Rider
Plain-English Description: Pays an extra amount if death is caused by an accident.
Example: A policy pays double the face amount after a fatal car crash.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Life Insurance Riders > Accidental Death Benefit Rider

Name: Waiver of Premium Rider
Plain-English Description: Stops premiums being due if the policyholder becomes totally disabled, keeping the cover in force.
Example: After a disabling stroke, the insured's policy stays active without further payments.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Life Insurance Riders > Waiver of Premium Rider

Name: Accelerated Death Benefit Rider
Plain-English Description: Lets a terminally, chronically or critically ill insured receive part of the death benefit while still alive.
Example: A patient given 6 months to live gets an advance on their policy to pay for care.
US Notes: Terminal illness acceleration is generally tax-free under the HIPAA 1996 rules.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Life Insurance Riders > Accelerated Death Benefit Rider

Name: Terminal Illness Rider
Plain-English Description: Pays part of the death benefit early if life expectancy is 12 or 24 months or less.
Example: A cancer patient receives 75% of the benefit early.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Life Insurance Riders > Accelerated Death Benefit Rider > Terminal Illness Rider

Name: Chronic Illness Rider
Plain-English Description: Pays part of the death benefit early if you can't perform 2 of 6 activities of daily living.
Example: A policyholder unable to bathe or dress unaided receives monthly payments.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Life Insurance Riders > Accelerated Death Benefit Rider > Chronic Illness Rider

Name: Critical Illness Rider
Plain-English Description: Pays part of the death benefit early on diagnosis of a listed condition such as heart attack or stroke.
Example: A policyholder draws $50,000 after a heart attack.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Life Insurance Riders > Accelerated Death Benefit Rider > Critical Illness Rider

Name: Long-Term Care Rider
Plain-English Description: Lets the death benefit be used to pay for long-term care costs, meeting federal tax-qualified LTC rules.
Example: An insured with dementia uses part of the death benefit to pay for memory care.
US Notes: Tax-qualified under IRC Section 7702B when it meets federal standards.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Life Insurance Riders > Long-Term Care Rider

Name: Child Term Rider
Plain-English Description: Adds small term cover for the policyholder's children.
Example: A parent adds $10,000 of cover for all children on their own policy.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Life Insurance Riders > Child Term Rider

Name: Guaranteed Insurability Rider
Plain-English Description: Lets you buy more cover at set times or life events without new medical checks.
Example: A policyholder increases cover after the birth of a child without a medical exam.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Life Insurance Riders > Guaranteed Insurability Rider

Name: Paid-Up Additions Rider
Plain-English Description: Lets you pay extra premium into a whole life policy to buy small amounts of fully paid-up cover, boosting cash value.
Example: A policyholder adds $5,000 a year of PUAs to grow cash value faster.
US Notes: Must be managed to avoid MEC status.
Full Path: Life Insurance > Life Insurance Riders > Paid-Up Additions Rider

Name: Health Insurance
Plain-English Description: Pays for medical care, or pays cash, when you are ill, injured or disabled.
Example: A family's plan pays most of the hospital bill when a child needs surgery.
US Notes: Private plans are regulated by states and by federal law (ACA, ERISA, HIPAA). Government programs are listed under Social & Government Programs.
Full Path: Health Insurance

Name: Major Medical (Comprehensive)
Plain-English Description: Comprehensive health cover for doctor visits, hospital stays, prescriptions and preventive care, bought individually or through an employer.
Example: A freelancer buys an individual plan on the marketplace.
US Notes: Under the ACA, major medical plans must cover 10 essential health benefits, can't deny pre-existing conditions, and have annual out-of-pocket maximums.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Major Medical (Comprehensive)

Name: Network Plan Types
Plain-English Description: Plan designs that control cost through provider networks and rules on referrals.
Example: An employee chooses between an HMO and a PPO during open enrollment.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Major Medical (Comprehensive) > Network Plan Types

Name: Health Maintenance Organization (HMO)
Plain-English Description: You must use the plan's network and usually need a referral from your primary care physician (PCP) to see a specialist; out-of-network care is not covered except emergencies.
Example: A family accepts a narrow network for lower premiums.
US Notes: Licensed under state HMO laws; example: Kaiser Permanente.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Major Medical (Comprehensive) > Network Plan Types > Health Maintenance Organization (HMO)

Name: Preferred Provider Organization (PPO)
Plain-English Description: You can see any doctor without referrals; in-network care costs less, and out-of-network care is partly covered.
Example: A person who travels a lot picks a PPO to see specialists anywhere.
US Notes: The most common plan type in employer coverage.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Major Medical (Comprehensive) > Network Plan Types > Preferred Provider Organization (PPO)

Name: Exclusive Provider Organization (EPO)
Plain-English Description: Like a PPO with no referrals, but only in-network care is covered (except emergencies).
Example: A worker happy with the local network picks an EPO to save money.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Major Medical (Comprehensive) > Network Plan Types > Exclusive Provider Organization (EPO)

Name: Point of Service (POS)
Plain-English Description: A hybrid: you choose a PCP and need referrals like an HMO, but can go out of network at higher cost like a PPO.
Example: A family wants a gatekeeper doctor with some out-of-network flexibility.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Major Medical (Comprehensive) > Network Plan Types > Point of Service (POS)

Name: High Deductible Health Plan (HDHP)
Plain-English Description: A plan with a high deductible and lower premium; it can be paired with a tax-advantaged Health Savings Account (HSA).
Example: A healthy 28-year-old picks an HDHP and saves the premium difference in an HSA.
US Notes: The IRS sets minimum deductibles and maximum out-of-pocket limits yearly for HSA eligibility.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Major Medical (Comprehensive) > Network Plan Types > High Deductible Health Plan (HDHP)

Name: Fee-for-Service Indemnity Plan
Plain-English Description: Pays a share of any provider's bills with no network; now rare and expensive.
Example: A patient sees any doctor and is reimbursed 80% after the deductible.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Major Medical (Comprehensive) > Network Plan Types > Fee-for-Service Indemnity Plan

Name: Individual Market Plans
Plain-English Description: Health plans people buy for themselves, on or off the government exchanges.
Example: A self-employed person compares plans on HealthCare.gov and qualifies for a subsidy.
US Notes: Sold on HealthCare.gov or a state-run exchange (e.g. Covered California). Premium tax credits are available on-exchange by income; the temporary 'enhanced' credits expired at the end of 2025, so from 2026 households above 400% of the federal poverty level again get no credit. Open enrollment starts Nov 1 each year (HealthCare.gov runs to Jan 15; state exchange dates vary).
Full Path: Health Insurance > Major Medical (Comprehensive) > Individual Market Plans

Name: Bronze Plan
Plain-English Description: Covers about 60% of average costs: lowest premium, highest out-of-pocket.
Example: A young healthy person wants protection mostly against large bills.
US Notes: Actuarial value approx. 60%.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Major Medical (Comprehensive) > Individual Market Plans > Bronze Plan

Name: Silver Plan
Plain-English Description: Covers about 70% of average costs; the only tier eligible for extra cost-sharing reductions for lower incomes.
Example: A low-income household picks silver to get reduced deductibles.
US Notes: The second-lowest-cost silver plan is the benchmark for subsidies.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Major Medical (Comprehensive) > Individual Market Plans > Silver Plan

Name: Silver 73% CSR Variant
Plain-English Description: A silver plan version with lower deductibles and copays (about 73% actuarial value) for enrollees with incomes of 200-250% of the federal poverty level.
Example: A household at 220% of poverty gets a lower deductible automatically.
US Notes: Cost-sharing reductions are available only on-exchange with a silver plan.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Major Medical (Comprehensive) > Individual Market Plans > Silver Plan > Silver 73% CSR Variant

Name: Silver 87% CSR Variant
Plain-English Description: A silver plan version with about 87% actuarial value for incomes of 150-200% of the federal poverty level.
Example: A single adult at 175% of poverty pays a much lower deductible.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Major Medical (Comprehensive) > Individual Market Plans > Silver Plan > Silver 87% CSR Variant

Name: Silver 94% CSR Variant
Plain-English Description: A silver plan version with about 94% actuarial value for incomes of 100-150% of the federal poverty level.
Example: A low-income worker gets near-platinum cost sharing at a silver price.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Major Medical (Comprehensive) > Individual Market Plans > Silver Plan > Silver 94% CSR Variant

Name: Gold Plan
Plain-English Description: Covers about 80% of average costs: higher premium, lower out-of-pocket.
Example: Someone with regular prescriptions picks gold.
US Notes: Actuarial value approx. 80%.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Major Medical (Comprehensive) > Individual Market Plans > Gold Plan

Name: Platinum Plan
Plain-English Description: Covers about 90% of average costs: highest premium, lowest out-of-pocket.
Example: A person expecting major surgery chooses platinum.
US Notes: Not offered in every state.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Major Medical (Comprehensive) > Individual Market Plans > Platinum Plan

Name: Catastrophic Plan
Plain-English Description: Very high deductible plan for people under 30 or with a hardship exemption; covers preventive care and 3 primary care visits before the deductible.
Example: A 25-year-old buys a catastrophic plan as a safety net.
US Notes: Not eligible for premium tax credits. Treated as HSA-eligible from 2026.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Major Medical (Comprehensive) > Individual Market Plans > Catastrophic Plan

Name: Employer Group Health
Plain-English Description: Health cover an employer offers to employees and their families, usually sharing the premium cost.
Example: A company covers employees and their dependents under one plan.
US Notes: The largest source of US health coverage. Employers with 50+ full-time employees face the ACA employer mandate.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Major Medical (Comprehensive) > Employer Group Health

Name: Fully Insured Plan
Plain-English Description: The employer pays premiums and the insurer carries the claims risk.
Example: A 50-person firm buys a standard group plan from an insurer.
US Notes: Subject to state insurance mandates.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Major Medical (Comprehensive) > Employer Group Health > Fully Insured Plan

Name: Self-Funded (ASO) Plan
Plain-English Description: The employer pays claims from its own funds and hires an insurer or third-party administrator (TPA) only to process them.
Example: A large retailer self-funds health claims to control costs.
US Notes: Governed by federal ERISA, which preempts most state insurance mandates.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Major Medical (Comprehensive) > Employer Group Health > Self-Funded (ASO) Plan

Name: Medical Stop-Loss
Plain-English Description: Protects a self-funded employer against very large individual claims (specific) or high total claims (aggregate).
Example: A self-funded employer is reimbursed for an employee's $1 million cancer treatment above a $150,000 deductible.
US Notes: Regulated by states as insurance to the employer, not as health insurance.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Major Medical (Comprehensive) > Employer Group Health > Medical Stop-Loss

Name: Level-Funded Plan
Plain-English Description: A small-business form of self-funding with fixed monthly payments that include stop-loss cover and possible year-end refunds.
Example: A 40-person company gets a refund when claims are lower than expected.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Major Medical (Comprehensive) > Employer Group Health > Level-Funded Plan

Name: Individual Coverage HRA (ICHRA)
Plain-English Description: The employer gives tax-free money that employees use to buy their own individual-market plans.
Example: A startup gives each employee $500 a month to buy a marketplace plan.
US Notes: Created by a 2019 federal rule, available from Jan 1, 2020.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Major Medical (Comprehensive) > Employer Group Health > Individual Coverage HRA (ICHRA)

Name: COBRA Continuation Coverage
Plain-English Description: Lets employees and families keep their employer group plan for a limited time (usually 18 months) after leaving a job, paying the full premium.
Example: A laid-off worker keeps the family on the group plan for 18 months.
US Notes: Federal law for employers with 20+ employees; many states have "mini-COBRA" laws for smaller employers.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Major Medical (Comprehensive) > Employer Group Health > COBRA Continuation Coverage

Name: Short-Term Limited-Duration Insurance (STLDI)
Plain-English Description: Temporary health cover that doesn't have to follow ACA rules, so it can exclude pre-existing conditions.
Example: Someone between jobs buys a 3-month plan.
US Notes: A 2024 federal rule limited STLDI to 3 months (4 months with renewals), but in August 2025 the federal agencies said they would not enforce those limits while they write a new rule. Some states restrict or ban it outright.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Major Medical (Comprehensive) > Short-Term Limited-Duration Insurance (STLDI)

Name: Health Care Sharing Ministries
Plain-English Description: Members of a faith-based group share each other's medical bills; this is not insurance and has no guarantee of payment.
Example: A family joins a sharing ministry and submits bills to be shared by members.
US Notes: Not regulated as insurance in most states; exempt from ACA rules.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Major Medical (Comprehensive) > Health Care Sharing Ministries

Name: Private Medicare Plans
Plain-English Description: Private insurance products that work with or replace federal Medicare benefits.
Example: A 65-year-old chooses between Medigap and a Medicare Advantage plan.
US Notes: Regulated by CMS (federal) plus state insurance departments for Medigap. Original Medicare itself is under Social & Government Programs.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Private Medicare Plans

Name: Medicare Advantage (Part C)
Plain-English Description: A private plan that replaces Original Medicare, often as an HMO or PPO, usually including drug coverage and extras like dental and vision.
Example: A retiree picks a $0-premium HMO Medicare Advantage plan with dental.
US Notes: Covers more than half of eligible Medicare beneficiaries (54% in 2025). Annual Medicare open enrollment runs Oct 15-Dec 7.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Private Medicare Plans > Medicare Advantage (Part C)

Name: Medicare Advantage HMO
Plain-English Description: A Medicare Advantage plan with a network and referrals.
Example: A retiree uses doctors in the plan's local network.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Private Medicare Plans > Medicare Advantage (Part C) > Medicare Advantage HMO

Name: Medicare Advantage PPO
Plain-English Description: A Medicare Advantage plan that also partly covers out-of-network care.
Example: A retiree who spends winters in another state picks a PPO.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Private Medicare Plans > Medicare Advantage (Part C) > Medicare Advantage PPO

Name: Special Needs Plan (SNP)
Plain-English Description: A Medicare Advantage plan for people who are also on Medicaid (D-SNP), have certain chronic conditions (C-SNP) or live in institutions (I-SNP).
Example: A low-income senior on both Medicare and Medicaid joins a D-SNP.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Private Medicare Plans > Medicare Advantage (Part C) > Special Needs Plan (SNP)

Name: Dual Eligible SNP (D-SNP)
Plain-English Description: For people who have both Medicare and Medicaid; coordinates benefits of the two programs.
Example: A low-income senior gets Medicare and Medicaid benefits through one plan.
US Notes: The largest SNP type.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Private Medicare Plans > Medicare Advantage (Part C) > Special Needs Plan (SNP) > Dual Eligible SNP (D-SNP)

Name: Chronic Condition SNP (C-SNP)
Plain-English Description: For people with specific severe chronic conditions such as diabetes, heart failure or ESRD.
Example: A retiree with heart failure joins a plan with specialised care coordination.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Private Medicare Plans > Medicare Advantage (Part C) > Special Needs Plan (SNP) > Chronic Condition SNP (C-SNP)

Name: Institutional SNP (I-SNP)
Plain-English Description: For people who live in nursing homes or need that level of care at home.
Example: A nursing home resident's plan provides on-site care teams.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Private Medicare Plans > Medicare Advantage (Part C) > Special Needs Plan (SNP) > Institutional SNP (I-SNP)

Name: Private Fee-for-Service (PFFS)
Plain-English Description: A Medicare Advantage plan that sets its own payment terms with any provider willing to accept them.
Example: Rare today; available in a few rural areas.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Private Medicare Plans > Medicare Advantage (Part C) > Private Fee-for-Service (PFFS)

Name: Medicare Medical Savings Account (MSA)
Plain-English Description: A high-deductible Medicare Advantage plan paired with a savings account funded by Medicare.
Example: A healthy retiree uses the deposit toward costs before the deductible.
US Notes: Limited availability.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Private Medicare Plans > Medicare Advantage (Part C) > Medicare Medical Savings Account (MSA)

Name: Medicare Part D (Prescription Drug Plan)
Plain-English Description: Standalone private plans that cover prescription drugs for people on Original Medicare.
Example: A retiree with Original Medicare adds a Part D plan for their medications.
US Notes: The Inflation Reduction Act capped Part D out-of-pocket drug spending at $2,000 in 2025; the cap is indexed and is $2,100 in 2026.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Private Medicare Plans > Medicare Part D (Prescription Drug Plan)

Name: Medicare Supplement (Medigap)
Plain-English Description: Private policies that pay gaps in Original Medicare, such as deductibles and 20% coinsurance, sold as standardized plans lettered A-N.
Example: A 66-year-old buys Medigap Plan G to limit out-of-pocket costs.
US Notes: Plans standardized by federal law; Massachusetts, Minnesota and Wisconsin use their own designs.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Private Medicare Plans > Medicare Supplement (Medigap)

Name: Medigap Plan G
Plain-English Description: Covers almost all gaps except the Part B deductible; the most popular plan for new enrollees.
Example: A new retiree picks Plan G for predictable costs.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Private Medicare Plans > Medicare Supplement (Medigap) > Medigap Plan G

Name: Medigap Plan N
Plain-English Description: Lower premium than G, with small copays for office and ER visits.
Example: A retiree who rarely sees a doctor picks Plan N.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Private Medicare Plans > Medicare Supplement (Medigap) > Medigap Plan N

Name: Medigap Plan F
Plain-English Description: Covers all gaps including the Part B deductible.
Example: A retiree eligible before 2020 keeps Plan F.
US Notes: Plans C and F are closed to people newly eligible for Medicare on or after Jan 1, 2020 (MACRA), because new plans can no longer cover the Part B deductible.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Private Medicare Plans > Medicare Supplement (Medigap) > Medigap Plan F

Name: High-Deductible Plan G
Plain-English Description: Same benefits as Plan G after a yearly deductible, for a much lower premium.
Example: A healthy retiree takes the high deductible to save on premiums.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Private Medicare Plans > Medicare Supplement (Medigap) > High-Deductible Plan G

Name: Supplemental Health (Voluntary Benefits)
Plain-English Description: Pays fixed cash amounts for specific events, on top of major medical, to help with out-of-pocket costs.
Example: A worker gets a cash payment after an accident to help cover the deductible.
US Notes: Commonly sold at the worksite through payroll deduction (e.g. Aflac, Colonial Life). "Excepted benefits" not subject to ACA rules.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Supplemental Health (Voluntary Benefits)

Name: Critical Illness Insurance
Plain-English Description: Pays a lump sum on diagnosis of a listed serious illness like cancer, heart attack or stroke.
Example: A woman diagnosed with breast cancer receives $20,000 to use as she wishes.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Supplemental Health (Voluntary Benefits) > Critical Illness Insurance

Name: Cancer Insurance
Plain-English Description: Pays benefits specifically for cancer diagnosis and treatment.
Example: A person with a family history of cancer buys a cancer-only policy.
US Notes: Some states prohibit or restrict disease-specific policies.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Supplemental Health (Voluntary Benefits) > Cancer Insurance

Name: Hospital Indemnity
Plain-English Description: Pays a fixed amount per day or per admission while hospitalized, regardless of actual bills.
Example: A patient gets $200 per day for a 5-day hospital stay.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Supplemental Health (Voluntary Benefits) > Hospital Indemnity

Name: Accident Insurance
Plain-English Description: Pays set amounts for injuries such as fractures, dislocations or ER visits caused by accidents.
Example: A child breaks an arm playing soccer and the family receives a fixed payment.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Supplemental Health (Voluntary Benefits) > Accident Insurance

Name: Accidental Death & Dismemberment (AD&D)
Plain-English Description: Pays fixed sums for accidental death or loss of limbs, sight, speech or hearing.
Example: An employee's family receives an AD&D benefit after a fatal work accident.
US Notes: Often bundled with group life.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Supplemental Health (Voluntary Benefits) > Accidental Death & Dismemberment (AD&D)

Name: Dental Insurance
Plain-English Description: Covers preventive, basic and major dental work, often with a yearly maximum.
Example: A family plan covers two cleanings a year and 50% of crowns.
US Notes: Often structured as DPPO or DHMO; pediatric dental is an ACA essential health benefit.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Supplemental Health (Voluntary Benefits) > Dental Insurance

Name: Dental PPO (DPPO)
Plain-English Description: Dental plan with a network but some out-of-network coverage.
Example: An employee keeps their current dentist who is out of network.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Supplemental Health (Voluntary Benefits) > Dental Insurance > Dental PPO (DPPO)

Name: Dental HMO (DHMO)
Plain-English Description: Low-cost dental plan requiring an assigned network dentist, with fixed copays.
Example: A family pays $10 copays at an assigned dentist.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Supplemental Health (Voluntary Benefits) > Dental Insurance > Dental HMO (DHMO)

Name: Vision Insurance
Plain-English Description: Covers eye exams and part of the cost of glasses or contact lenses.
Example: An employee gets a yearly eye exam and a $150 frame allowance.
US Notes: Major carriers include VSP and EyeMed.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Supplemental Health (Voluntary Benefits) > Vision Insurance

Name: Disability Insurance
Plain-English Description: Replaces part of your income if illness or injury stops you from working.
Example: A surgeon who injures a hand receives 60% of her income until she recovers.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Disability Insurance

Name: Short-Term Disability (STD)
Plain-English Description: Pays part of your salary for a short period, typically 3 to 6 months, after a short waiting period.
Example: An employee on leave after surgery gets 60% pay for 8 weeks.
US Notes: Mandatory state programs exist in CA, HI, NJ, NY, RI and PR (see Social & Government Programs).
Full Path: Health Insurance > Disability Insurance > Short-Term Disability (STD)

Name: Long-Term Disability (LTD)
Plain-English Description: Pays part of your salary for long periods, often until retirement age, after a waiting period (often 90 days).
Example: A worker with a serious back injury receives benefits for years.
US Notes: Group LTD claims are governed by ERISA.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Disability Insurance > Long-Term Disability (LTD)

Name: Own-Occupation Definition
Plain-English Description: Pays if you can't do your own specific job, even if you could do another job.
Example: A dentist with a hand tremor is paid even though she could teach.
US Notes: Common in individual policies for physicians and dentists.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Disability Insurance > Long-Term Disability (LTD) > Own-Occupation Definition

Name: Any-Occupation Definition
Plain-English Description: Pays only if you can't do any job you're reasonably suited for by education and experience; cheaper but harder to claim.
Example: Benefits stop because the person could still do desk work.
US Notes: Group LTD often switches from own-occ to any-occ after 24 months.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Disability Insurance > Long-Term Disability (LTD) > Any-Occupation Definition

Name: Individual Disability Income
Plain-English Description: A disability policy owned by the individual, portable between jobs, often non-cancelable with guaranteed premiums.
Example: A self-employed lawyer buys an IDI policy.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Disability Insurance > Individual Disability Income

Name: Business Overhead Expense (BOE)
Plain-English Description: Pays a small business's fixed expenses (rent, staff wages) while the owner is disabled.
Example: A dentist's rent and staff salaries are paid during recovery.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Disability Insurance > Business Overhead Expense (BOE)

Name: Disability Buy-Out
Plain-English Description: Funds the purchase of a disabled business owner's share by the other owners.
Example: Partners buy out a colleague who became permanently disabled.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Disability Insurance > Disability Buy-Out

Name: Long-Term Care Insurance
Plain-English Description: Pays for help with daily living (bathing, dressing, eating) at home, in assisted living or in a nursing home.
Example: An 80-year-old with Alzheimer's has nursing home fees paid by her LTC policy.
US Notes: Medicare does not cover long-term custodial care; Medicaid does but only after assets are spent down.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Long-Term Care Insurance

Name: Traditional Standalone LTC
Plain-English Description: A policy that pays only for long-term care, with premiums that can rise over time.
Example: A 55-year-old buys standalone LTC for future care.
US Notes: Many older blocks have seen large state-approved rate increases.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Long-Term Care Insurance > Traditional Standalone LTC

Name: Hybrid Life/LTC
Plain-English Description: Life insurance or an annuity with long-term care benefits built in, so money is paid either for care or at death.
Example: A couple buys a hybrid so their premiums aren't "lost" if they never need care.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Long-Term Care Insurance > Hybrid Life/LTC

Name: Long-Term Care Partnership Policy
Plain-English Description: A qualifying LTC policy that lets you keep extra assets and still qualify for Medicaid if you use up your benefits.
Example: A buyer protects $300,000 of assets by buying a Partnership policy with $300,000 of benefits.
US Notes: Available in most states under the Deficit Reduction Act of 2005.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Long-Term Care Insurance > Long-Term Care Partnership Policy

Name: Tax-Advantaged Health Accounts
Plain-English Description: Savings or reimbursement accounts that pay medical costs with pre-tax money. They are not insurance but are closely linked to health plans.
Example: An employee pays a deductible from an HSA.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Tax-Advantaged Health Accounts

Name: Health Savings Account (HSA)
Plain-English Description: A personal savings account for medical costs, only available with an HSA-eligible HDHP; money rolls over and can be invested.
Example: A worker contributes $4,000 a year and invests the balance.
US Notes: Contribution limits set yearly by the IRS; triple tax advantage. From 2026, all bronze and catastrophic plans count as HSA-eligible, and people with certain direct primary care arrangements can contribute (One Big Beautiful Bill Act; IRS Notice 2026-5).
Full Path: Health Insurance > Tax-Advantaged Health Accounts > Health Savings Account (HSA)

Name: Flexible Spending Account (FSA)
Plain-English Description: An employer account funded by pre-tax salary for medical costs; unused money is mostly lost at year end.
Example: An employee sets aside $2,000 for glasses and copays.
US Notes: Limited carryover or grace period allowed by IRS.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Tax-Advantaged Health Accounts > Flexible Spending Account (FSA)

Name: Health Reimbursement Arrangement (HRA)
Plain-English Description: An employer-funded account that reimburses employees' medical costs.
Example: An employer reimburses up to $1,500 of deductible costs.
Full Path: Health Insurance > Tax-Advantaged Health Accounts > Health Reimbursement Arrangement (HRA)

Name: Home & Personal Property Insurance
Also Known As: Home insurance; Homeowners and renters insurance
Plain-English Description: Pays to repair or replace homes and belongings that are damaged, destroyed or stolen. This branch covers personal (household) property; business property is under Commercial Lines.
Example: A homeowner claims for repairs after a kitchen fire.
US Notes: Regulated by states. Most standard forms come from ISO (Insurance Services Office); some insurers use their own or AAIS forms.
Full Path: Home & Personal Property Insurance

Name: Homeowners Insurance (HO Forms)
Plain-English Description: Package policy for homes that combines cover for the dwelling, other structures, belongings, loss of use (extra living costs) and personal liability. The current ISO homeowners forms are HO-2, HO-3, HO-4, HO-5, HO-6 and HO-8; HO-1 has been withdrawn in nearly all states, and 'HO-7' is an industry label for mobile home cover, not an ISO form.
Example: A family's HO-3 pays to rebuild the roof after a storm and to put them up in a hotel.
US Notes: Not legally required, but mortgage lenders require it. Coverage parts are labelled A (Dwelling), B (Other Structures), C (Personal Property), D (Loss of Use), E (Personal Liability), F (Medical Payments).
Full Path: Home & Personal Property Insurance > Homeowners Insurance (HO Forms)

Name: HO-1 Basic Form
Plain-English Description: Covers the house against a short named list of perils such as fire, lightning, windstorm and theft.
Example: Offered as a bare-minimum option.
US Notes: Rarely offered today; unavailable in most states.
Full Path: Home & Personal Property Insurance > Homeowners Insurance (HO Forms) > HO-1 Basic Form

Name: HO-2 Broad Form
Plain-English Description: Covers the house and belongings against a longer named list of perils, including falling objects, weight of snow and burst pipes.
Example: A buyer wants cheaper named-peril cover rather than open-peril.
Full Path: Home & Personal Property Insurance > Homeowners Insurance (HO Forms) > HO-2 Broad Form

Name: HO-3 Special Form
Plain-English Description: The most common US home policy: the house is covered for all causes of loss except those excluded (open perils), while belongings are covered for named perils.
Example: Most mortgage-holding homeowners have an HO-3.
US Notes: Accounts for the large majority of US homeowners policies. Flood and earthquake are excluded.
Full Path: Home & Personal Property Insurance > Homeowners Insurance (HO Forms) > HO-3 Special Form

Name: HO-4 Renters Insurance
Plain-English Description: Covers a renter's belongings, liability and extra living expenses, but not the building.
Example: A student's laptop is stolen from an apartment and replaced by the renters policy.
US Notes: Many landlords require it in the lease.
Full Path: Home & Personal Property Insurance > Homeowners Insurance (HO Forms) > HO-4 Renters Insurance

Name: HO-5 Comprehensive Form
Plain-English Description: Open-peril cover for both the house and belongings, the broadest protection.
Example: A homeowner with valuable furnishings chooses HO-5.
Full Path: Home & Personal Property Insurance > Homeowners Insurance (HO Forms) > HO-5 Comprehensive Form

Name: HO-6 Condo Insurance
Plain-English Description: Covers a condo owner's belongings, interior walls, fixtures and improvements, and liability; the building shell is covered by the association's master policy.
Example: A condo owner claims for new kitchen cabinets after a pipe burst.
US Notes: Coverage needed depends on the HOA's master policy ("bare walls" vs "all-in").
Full Path: Home & Personal Property Insurance > Homeowners Insurance (HO Forms) > HO-6 Condo Insurance

Name: Loss Assessment Coverage
Plain-English Description: Pays your share of a special assessment the condo or HOA charges owners after a covered loss to common property.
Example: The HOA charges each owner $5,000 after lobby fire damage exceeds its policy.
Full Path: Home & Personal Property Insurance > Homeowners Insurance (HO Forms) > HO-6 Condo Insurance > Loss Assessment Coverage

Name: Mobile / Manufactured Home Insurance
Plain-English Description: Covers mobile and manufactured homes, which often need specialised cover.
Example: A retiree insures a manufactured home in a park.
US Notes: Many insurers use their own mobile home forms or an endorsement to HO-2/HO-3.
Full Path: Home & Personal Property Insurance > Homeowners Insurance (HO Forms) > Mobile / Manufactured Home Insurance

Name: HO-8 Modified Coverage Form
Plain-English Description: For older homes whose rebuilding cost is far above market value; pays for repair using standard materials or actual cash value.
Example: A 1900s house with ornate plaster is insured under an HO-8.
Full Path: Home & Personal Property Insurance > Homeowners Insurance (HO Forms) > HO-8 Modified Coverage Form

Name: Homeowners Endorsements
Plain-English Description: Optional changes to a home policy that add or broaden cover.
Example: A homeowner adds sewer backup and replacement cost for contents.
Full Path: Home & Personal Property Insurance > Homeowners Endorsements

Name: Water Backup & Sump Overflow
Plain-English Description: Covers damage when water backs up through drains or a sump pump fails. Excluded by default.
Example: A basement floods from a sewer backup during a heavy storm.
Full Path: Home & Personal Property Insurance > Homeowners Endorsements > Water Backup & Sump Overflow

Name: Service Line Coverage
Plain-English Description: Covers repair of buried utility lines (water, sewer, power) on your property.
Example: A cracked sewer line under the lawn is replaced.
Full Path: Home & Personal Property Insurance > Homeowners Endorsements > Service Line Coverage

Name: Replacement Cost on Contents
Plain-English Description: Pays to replace belongings with new ones rather than their depreciated value.
Example: A 5-year-old sofa is replaced with a new equivalent.
Full Path: Home & Personal Property Insurance > Homeowners Endorsements > Replacement Cost on Contents

Name: Extended / Guaranteed Replacement Cost
Plain-English Description: Pays extra (e.g. 125%) or the full cost to rebuild if costs exceed the dwelling limit.
Example: Construction costs surge after a wildfire, and the extra 25% covers the gap.
US Notes: Guaranteed replacement cost has become rare.
Full Path: Home & Personal Property Insurance > Homeowners Endorsements > Extended / Guaranteed Replacement Cost

Name: Ordinance or Law Coverage
Plain-English Description: Pays extra rebuilding costs to meet current building codes.
Example: A rebuilt home must meet new electrical codes.
Full Path: Home & Personal Property Insurance > Homeowners Endorsements > Ordinance or Law Coverage

Name: Home Business Endorsement
Plain-English Description: Adds cover for business property and liability for small businesses run from home.
Example: A home bakery adds cover for its equipment and customers.
Full Path: Home & Personal Property Insurance > Homeowners Endorsements > Home Business Endorsement

Name: Identity Fraud Expense
Plain-English Description: Pays costs to restore your identity after identity theft.
Example: Fees and lost wages from fixing credit reports are reimbursed.
Full Path: Home & Personal Property Insurance > Homeowners Endorsements > Identity Fraud Expense

Name: Dwelling Fire Policies (DP Forms)
Plain-English Description: Policies for homes that aren't owner-occupied, such as rentals or vacant homes, covering the building but not the tenant's belongings.
Example: A landlord insures a rented house with a DP-3.
US Notes: Liability is usually added by endorsement or a separate policy.
Full Path: Home & Personal Property Insurance > Dwelling Fire Policies (DP Forms)

Name: DP-1 Basic Form
Plain-English Description: Named perils (fire, lightning, internal explosion) with optional extended coverage, usually paid at actual cash value.
Example: A cheap policy for a vacant cabin.
Full Path: Home & Personal Property Insurance > Dwelling Fire Policies (DP Forms) > DP-1 Basic Form

Name: DP-2 Broad Form
Plain-English Description: Broader named perils, usually paid at replacement cost.
Example: A small landlord wants mid-level cover.
Full Path: Home & Personal Property Insurance > Dwelling Fire Policies (DP Forms) > DP-2 Broad Form

Name: DP-3 Special Form
Plain-English Description: Open-peril cover for the dwelling at replacement cost, the most common landlord form.
Example: An investor insures three rental homes on DP-3.
Full Path: Home & Personal Property Insurance > Dwelling Fire Policies (DP Forms) > DP-3 Special Form

Name: Natural Catastrophe Coverage
Plain-English Description: Separate or add-on cover for natural disasters that standard home policies exclude or limit.
Example: A coastal homeowner buys separate flood and windstorm policies.
Full Path: Home & Personal Property Insurance > Natural Catastrophe Coverage

Name: Flood Insurance
Plain-English Description: Covers damage from rising water and surface flooding, which almost all homeowners policies exclude.
Example: A Houston family's flood policy pays after a hurricane floods their ground floor.
US Notes: Lenders require flood insurance for federally backed mortgages in FEMA Special Flood Hazard Areas.
Full Path: Home & Personal Property Insurance > Natural Catastrophe Coverage > Flood Insurance

Name: National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP)
Plain-English Description: The federal flood program run by FEMA, sold through private insurers ("Write Your Own") and agents. Covers up to $250,000 for a home's building and $100,000 for contents.
Example: A homeowner in a flood zone buys NFIP cover required by the lender.
US Notes: Premiums set by FEMA's Risk Rating 2.0 method; usually a 30-day waiting period. The program needs periodic reauthorization by Congress (most recently extended to Dec 11, 2026); if it lapses, FEMA pays claims but cannot sell or renew policies.
Full Path: Home & Personal Property Insurance > Natural Catastrophe Coverage > Flood Insurance > National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP)

Name: Private Flood Insurance
Plain-English Description: Flood cover from private insurers, often with higher limits, shorter waits or extra living expenses.
Example: A high-value home buys private flood for cover above NFIP limits.
US Notes: Lenders must accept qualifying private flood policies under federal rules.
Full Path: Home & Personal Property Insurance > Natural Catastrophe Coverage > Flood Insurance > Private Flood Insurance

Name: Earthquake Insurance
Plain-English Description: Covers damage from earthquakes, typically with a deductible of 5-25% of the dwelling limit.
Example: A Seattle homeowner adds earthquake cover with a 15% deductible.
US Notes: Available as an endorsement or separate policy in most states.
Full Path: Home & Personal Property Insurance > Natural Catastrophe Coverage > Earthquake Insurance

Name: California Earthquake Authority (CEA)
Plain-English Description: A publicly managed, privately funded body that writes most residential earthquake insurance in California.
Example: A homeowner in Los Angeles buys CEA cover through their home insurer.
US Notes: California insurers must offer earthquake cover to homeowners every two years.
Full Path: Home & Personal Property Insurance > Natural Catastrophe Coverage > Earthquake Insurance > California Earthquake Authority (CEA)

Name: Windstorm / Hurricane Coverage
Plain-English Description: Covers wind and hurricane damage. In some coastal areas wind is excluded from home policies and must be bought separately.
Example: A Texas coastal homeowner buys wind cover from the state wind pool.
US Notes: State residual markets include Citizens Property Insurance (FL), TWIA (TX) and other coastal plans. Hurricane deductibles are often a percentage of the dwelling limit.
Full Path: Home & Personal Property Insurance > Natural Catastrophe Coverage > Windstorm / Hurricane Coverage

Name: FAIR Plans
Also Known As: Fair Access to Insurance Requirements Plan
Plain-English Description: State-created insurers of last resort for property owners who can't get cover in the regular market, often due to wildfire or urban risk.
Example: A California homeowner dropped by their insurer gets fire cover from the California FAIR Plan.
US Notes: About 33 states plus DC have FAIR plans; usually named-peril cover that may need a separate 'difference in conditions' policy.
Full Path: Home & Personal Property Insurance > Natural Catastrophe Coverage > FAIR Plans

Name: Sinkhole Coverage
Plain-English Description: Covers damage from ground collapsing into underground cavities.
Example: A Florida home cracks from a sinkhole and the add-on pays for repairs.
US Notes: Florida policies must include catastrophic ground cover collapse; full sinkhole cover is optional.
Full Path: Home & Personal Property Insurance > Natural Catastrophe Coverage > Sinkhole Coverage

Name: Scheduled Personal Property
Plain-English Description: Extra cover for high-value items like jewelry, art and collectibles, usually with no deductible and worldwide open-peril cover.
Example: An engagement ring worth $15,000 is listed on a floater.
US Notes: Standard homeowners policies have low sub-limits (e.g. $1,500) for theft of jewelry.
Full Path: Home & Personal Property Insurance > Scheduled Personal Property

Name: Jewelry Coverage
Plain-English Description: Covers rings, watches and other jewelry against loss, theft and damage, including mysterious disappearance.
Example: A lost diamond earring is replaced.
Full Path: Home & Personal Property Insurance > Scheduled Personal Property > Jewelry Coverage

Name: Fine Art & Collectibles
Plain-English Description: Covers paintings, sculptures, wine and collections at agreed values.
Example: A collector insures a painting for its appraised value.
Full Path: Home & Personal Property Insurance > Scheduled Personal Property > Fine Art & Collectibles

Name: Musical Instruments
Plain-English Description: Covers instruments on and off premises, including while travelling.
Example: A cellist's instrument is damaged on a flight.
Full Path: Home & Personal Property Insurance > Scheduled Personal Property > Musical Instruments

Name: Device / Cell Phone Protection
Plain-English Description: Covers phones, laptops and other devices against damage, theft and breakdown.
Example: A cracked phone screen is repaired.
US Notes: Often sold by carriers and retailers; some plans are service contracts rather than insurance.
Full Path: Home & Personal Property Insurance > Scheduled Personal Property > Device / Cell Phone Protection

Name: High-Net-Worth Homeowners
Plain-English Description: Premium home programs for expensive homes and collections, with broader cover, cash settlement options and higher limits.
Example: A family with a $5 million home buys a private client policy.
US Notes: Written by specialist carriers such as Chubb, PURE and AIG Private Client.
Full Path: Home & Personal Property Insurance > High-Net-Worth Homeowners

Name: Home Warranty
Plain-English Description: A service contract that pays to repair or replace home systems and appliances that break from normal wear.
Example: A home warranty pays to fix a failed furnace in winter.
US Notes: Regulated as service contracts rather than insurance in many states.
Full Path: Home & Personal Property Insurance > Home Warranty

Name: Casualty & Liability Insurance
Plain-English Description: Pays for injury or damage you cause to other people or their property, including legal defense costs.
Example: A shop pays nothing out of pocket when a customer slips and sues, because its liability policy covers it.
US Notes: Liability rules (negligence, damages caps, joint and several liability) vary by state tort law.
Full Path: Casualty & Liability Insurance

Name: Personal Liability
Plain-English Description: Liability cover for individuals and families for accidents in daily life.
Example: A dog bites a neighbor and the owner's policy pays the medical bills.
Full Path: Casualty & Liability Insurance > Personal Liability

Name: Homeowners Liability (Coverage E)
Plain-English Description: Liability cover included in home and renters policies for injuries on your property or caused by you anywhere.
Example: A guest trips on a loose step and the homeowners policy pays the claim.
US Notes: Typical limits $100,000-$500,000.
Full Path: Casualty & Liability Insurance > Personal Liability > Homeowners Liability (Coverage E)

Name: Medical Payments to Others (Coverage F)
Plain-English Description: Pays small medical bills of guests injured on your property regardless of fault, to avoid lawsuits.
Example: A visiting child's stitches after a fall are paid.
US Notes: Typical limits $1,000-$5,000.
Full Path: Casualty & Liability Insurance > Personal Liability > Medical Payments to Others (Coverage F)

Name: Personal Umbrella
Plain-English Description: Extra liability cover (often $1 million or more) above your home and auto limits.
Example: A driver causes a serious crash and the umbrella pays the amount above the auto limit.
US Notes: Insurers usually require minimum underlying auto and home limits.
Full Path: Casualty & Liability Insurance > Personal Liability > Personal Umbrella

Name: Watercraft Liability
Plain-English Description: Liability cover for injuries or damage caused while operating a boat or jet ski.
Example: A jet-ski rider injures a swimmer and the policy pays.
US Notes: Home policies cover only small boats; larger craft need a boat policy.
Full Path: Casualty & Liability Insurance > Personal Liability > Watercraft Liability

Name: Canine Liability
Plain-English Description: Standalone liability for dog owners whose breed or history is excluded by their home insurer.
Example: An owner of an excluded breed buys a separate canine liability policy.
US Notes: Some insurers exclude certain breeds; several states restrict breed-based underwriting.
Full Path: Casualty & Liability Insurance > Personal Liability > Canine Liability

Name: Commercial General Liability (CGL)
Plain-English Description: Covers a business against third-party claims for bodily injury, property damage, and personal and advertising injury.
Example: A cafe pays a customer's claim after they burn themselves on a faulty cup.
US Notes: Standard ISO CG 00 01 (occurrence) and CG 00 02 (claims-made) forms. Commonly required in leases and contracts.
Full Path: Casualty & Liability Insurance > Commercial General Liability (CGL)

Name: Coverage A: Bodily Injury & Property Damage
Plain-English Description: Pays for injuries and damage your business causes to others.
Example: A contractor's worker drops a beam on a client's car.
Full Path: Casualty & Liability Insurance > Commercial General Liability (CGL) > Coverage A: Bodily Injury & Property Damage

Name: Premises & Operations
Plain-English Description: Covers injuries or damage on your premises or from your ongoing work.
Example: A shopper slips on a wet floor in a supermarket.
Full Path: Casualty & Liability Insurance > Commercial General Liability (CGL) > Coverage A: Bodily Injury & Property Damage > Premises & Operations

Name: Products & Completed Operations
Plain-English Description: Covers injuries or damage caused by products you made or sold, or work you finished.
Example: A toaster manufacturer is sued after a product catches fire.
US Notes: Subject to its own aggregate limit.
Full Path: Casualty & Liability Insurance > Commercial General Liability (CGL) > Coverage A: Bodily Injury & Property Damage > Products & Completed Operations

Name: Coverage B: Personal & Advertising Injury
Plain-English Description: Covers claims like libel, slander, false arrest and copyright infringement in advertising.
Example: A competitor sues over a misleading ad.
Full Path: Casualty & Liability Insurance > Commercial General Liability (CGL) > Coverage B: Personal & Advertising Injury

Name: Coverage C: Medical Payments
Plain-English Description: Pays small medical bills for people hurt on your premises regardless of fault.
Example: A customer's ER visit after tripping is paid.
Full Path: Casualty & Liability Insurance > Commercial General Liability (CGL) > Coverage C: Medical Payments

Name: Occurrence Form
Plain-English Description: Covers incidents that happen during the policy period, even if the claim is made years later.
Example: A claim for a 2022 injury filed in 2025 is paid by the 2022 policy.
US Notes: The standard for most CGL policies.
Full Path: Casualty & Liability Insurance > Commercial General Liability (CGL) > Occurrence Form

Name: Claims-Made Form
Plain-English Description: Covers claims first made during the policy period, subject to a retroactive date; tail cover extends the reporting window.
Example: A claim made in 2025 is handled by the 2025 policy.
Full Path: Casualty & Liability Insurance > Commercial General Liability (CGL) > Claims-Made Form

Name: Specialty Casualty Lines
Plain-English Description: Liability covers for specific exposures that CGL excludes or limits.
Example: A bar buys liquor liability because GL excludes it.
Full Path: Casualty & Liability Insurance > Specialty Casualty Lines

Name: Standalone Products Liability
Plain-English Description: Products liability written separately for manufacturers and distributors with large product exposures.
Example: A medical device maker buys dedicated products cover.
Full Path: Casualty & Liability Insurance > Specialty Casualty Lines > Standalone Products Liability

Name: Product Recall
Plain-English Description: Pays the costs of recalling faulty or contaminated products, and sometimes lost profits.
Example: A food maker recalls a batch contaminated with listeria.
US Notes: Recalls may be ordered by FDA, USDA, CPSC or NHTSA.
Full Path: Casualty & Liability Insurance > Specialty Casualty Lines > Product Recall

Name: Liquor Liability
Plain-English Description: Covers bars, restaurants and liquor stores against claims that alcohol they served led to injury.
Example: A bar is sued after an intoxicated customer causes a crash.
US Notes: Dram shop laws in many states make businesses that serve alcohol liable for harm caused by intoxicated customers, and some states (e.g. Minnesota) require liquor licensees to prove liability cover. The CGL excludes this risk for businesses that make, sell or serve alcohol.
Full Path: Casualty & Liability Insurance > Specialty Casualty Lines > Liquor Liability

Name: Environmental / Pollution Liability
Plain-English Description: Covers clean-up costs and third-party claims from pollution, which CGL mostly excludes.
Example: A factory's chemical leak into a river is cleaned up under the policy.
US Notes: Exposure driven by federal CERCLA (Superfund) and state environmental laws.
Full Path: Casualty & Liability Insurance > Specialty Casualty Lines > Environmental / Pollution Liability

Name: Contractors Pollution Liability (CPL)
Plain-English Description: Covers pollution caused by a contractor's work at job sites.
Example: A contractor disturbs asbestos and must pay for cleanup.
Full Path: Casualty & Liability Insurance > Specialty Casualty Lines > Environmental / Pollution Liability > Contractors Pollution Liability (CPL)

Name: Storage Tank Liability
Plain-English Description: Covers leaks from underground or aboveground fuel tanks.
Example: A gas station's leaking underground tank contaminates soil.
US Notes: EPA requires financial responsibility for underground storage tank owners.
Full Path: Casualty & Liability Insurance > Specialty Casualty Lines > Environmental / Pollution Liability > Storage Tank Liability

Name: Owners & Contractors Protective (OCP)
Plain-English Description: Covers a project owner for liability arising from a contractor's work, bought by the contractor.
Example: A city requires a road contractor to buy OCP naming the city.
Full Path: Casualty & Liability Insurance > Specialty Casualty Lines > Owners & Contractors Protective (OCP)

Name: Railroad Protective Liability
Plain-English Description: Covers a railroad for liability from contractors working on or near its tracks.
Example: A contractor building a bridge over rail lines buys this for the railroad.
Full Path: Casualty & Liability Insurance > Specialty Casualty Lines > Railroad Protective Liability

Name: Special Event Liability
Plain-English Description: Short-term liability for one-off events.
Example: A nonprofit gala buys one-day liability cover required by the venue.
Full Path: Casualty & Liability Insurance > Specialty Casualty Lines > Special Event Liability

Name: Workers' Compensation & Employers' Liability
Plain-English Description: Covers employees who are injured or become ill because of their work, paying medical bills and lost wages regardless of fault; in exchange, employees generally can't sue the employer.
Example: A roofer who falls from a ladder receives medical care and weekly wage benefits.
US Notes: Required by state law in every state except Texas (where it is optional). Benefits and rules set by each state. Standard NCCI policy form.
Full Path: Casualty & Liability Insurance > Workers' Compensation & Employers' Liability

Name: Part One: Workers' Compensation
Plain-English Description: Pays the benefits required by state workers' comp law: medical care, wage replacement, rehabilitation and death benefits.
Example: An injured warehouse worker gets two-thirds of wages while off work.
Full Path: Casualty & Liability Insurance > Workers' Compensation & Employers' Liability > Part One: Workers' Compensation

Name: Part Two: Employers' Liability
Plain-English Description: Covers lawsuits by employees or others (e.g. spouses) related to work injuries that fall outside the workers' comp system.
Example: An injured worker's spouse sues for loss of consortium.
Full Path: Casualty & Liability Insurance > Workers' Compensation & Employers' Liability > Part Two: Employers' Liability

Name: Part Three: Other States Coverage
Plain-English Description: Extends cover when employees work in states not listed on the policy.
Example: An employee is injured on a project in another state.
Full Path: Casualty & Liability Insurance > Workers' Compensation & Employers' Liability > Part Three: Other States Coverage

Name: Monopolistic State Funds
Plain-English Description: In four states, employers must buy workers' comp from the state fund rather than private insurers.
Example: An Ohio employer buys cover from the Ohio Bureau of Workers' Compensation.
US Notes: Ohio, Washington, North Dakota and Wyoming. Employers there buy "stop gap" employers' liability separately.
Full Path: Casualty & Liability Insurance > Workers' Compensation & Employers' Liability > Monopolistic State Funds

Name: Competitive State Funds
Plain-English Description: State-run workers' comp insurers that compete with private insurers and often act as the insurer of last resort.
Example: A small contractor denied by private carriers gets cover from the state fund.
US Notes: Examples: SCIF (California), NYSIF (New York), Texas Mutual (created by the Texas legislature and now a private mutual that acts as the state's insurer of last resort).
Full Path: Casualty & Liability Insurance > Workers' Compensation & Employers' Liability > Competitive State Funds

Name: Assigned Risk / Residual Market
Plain-English Description: A pool that provides workers' comp to employers that can't get it in the voluntary market.
Example: A new roofing firm with no history is placed in the assigned risk plan.
US Notes: Administered by NCCI in many states.
Full Path: Casualty & Liability Insurance > Workers' Compensation & Employers' Liability > Assigned Risk / Residual Market

Name: Federal Workers' Compensation Programs
Plain-English Description: Federal laws that replace state workers' comp for certain workers.
Example: A dock worker is covered under the Longshore Act.
Full Path: Casualty & Liability Insurance > Workers' Compensation & Employers' Liability > Federal Workers' Compensation Programs

Name: USL&H (Longshore) Coverage
Also Known As: Longshore and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act
Plain-English Description: Covers maritime workers like dock workers and ship repairers not covered by state comp.
Example: A shipyard worker injured on a pier is covered.
US Notes: Federal (Department of Labor).
Full Path: Casualty & Liability Insurance > Workers' Compensation & Employers' Liability > Federal Workers' Compensation Programs > USL&H (Longshore) Coverage

Name: Jones Act / Maritime Employers Liability
Plain-English Description: Covers seamen (crew members), who sue their employer under the Jones Act rather than using workers' comp.
Example: A deckhand injured on a tugboat claims under the Jones Act.
Full Path: Casualty & Liability Insurance > Workers' Compensation & Employers' Liability > Federal Workers' Compensation Programs > Jones Act / Maritime Employers Liability

Name: FECA (Federal Employees)
Plain-English Description: Covers federal government employees' work injuries.
Example: A postal worker hurt on the job receives FECA benefits.
US Notes: Administered by the Department of Labor; not bought from insurers.
Full Path: Casualty & Liability Insurance > Workers' Compensation & Employers' Liability > Federal Workers' Compensation Programs > FECA (Federal Employees)

Name: Defense Base Act (DBA)
Plain-English Description: Covers civilian contractors working overseas on US government contracts.
Example: A contractor employee injured at an overseas base is covered.
US Notes: Extension of the Longshore Act.
Full Path: Casualty & Liability Insurance > Workers' Compensation & Employers' Liability > Federal Workers' Compensation Programs > Defense Base Act (DBA)

Name: Occupational Accident Insurance
Plain-English Description: Accident cover for independent contractors, such as owner-operator truckers, who aren't eligible for workers' comp.
Example: An owner-operator trucker injured while loading gets medical and disability benefits.
Full Path: Casualty & Liability Insurance > Workers' Compensation & Employers' Liability > Occupational Accident Insurance

Name: PEO Workers' Comp
Plain-English Description: Workers' comp provided through a Professional Employer Organization that co-employs a small business's staff.
Example: A small company gets workers' comp through its PEO.
Full Path: Casualty & Liability Insurance > Workers' Compensation & Employers' Liability > PEO Workers' Comp
