Name: Commercial Umbrella & Excess Liability
Plain-English Description: Extra liability limits above primary general liability, auto and employers' liability policies.
Example: A trucking company buys $10 million of excess cover above its primary auto policy.
Full Path: Casualty & Liability Insurance > Commercial Umbrella & Excess Liability

Name: Commercial Umbrella
Plain-English Description: Adds limits above several primary policies and may cover some gaps they leave, after a self-insured retention.
Example: A manufacturer buys a $5 million umbrella over GL, auto and EL.
Full Path: Casualty & Liability Insurance > Commercial Umbrella & Excess Liability > Commercial Umbrella

Name: Follow-Form Excess
Plain-English Description: Adds limits using exactly the same terms as the underlying policy.
Example: A second $10 million layer follows the umbrella's terms.
US Notes: Large programs stack several excess layers into a "tower".
Full Path: Casualty & Liability Insurance > Commercial Umbrella & Excess Liability > Follow-Form Excess

Name: Legal Expense Insurance
Plain-English Description: Pays for access to lawyers for personal legal matters such as wills, traffic tickets and disputes.
Example: An employee uses a prepaid legal plan to draft a will.
US Notes: Often offered as a voluntary employee benefit; regulated differently by state.
Full Path: Casualty & Liability Insurance > Legal Expense Insurance

Name: Auto Insurance
Plain-English Description: Covers vehicles and drivers for damage to the vehicle, injuries, and harm caused to others. Some liability cover is legally required in nearly every state.
Example: A driver's policy pays for another car's repairs after a rear-end collision.
US Notes: Minimum liability limits, no-fault rules and required coverages are set by each state. New Hampshire does not require auto insurance for most drivers but requires proof of financial responsibility after a crash.
Full Path: Auto Insurance

Name: Personal Auto Policy (PAP)
Plain-English Description: Cover for cars, SUVs, pickups and minivans owned and used by individuals.
Example: A commuter insures the family SUV.
US Notes: Based on the ISO Personal Auto Policy form in many states.
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Personal Auto Policy (PAP)

Name: Liability Coverage
Plain-English Description: Pays for injury and damage you cause to others; the legal minimum in almost every state. It doesn't pay for your own car.
Example: An owner of an old car buys only liability cover.
US Notes: Limits are written as split limits such as 25/50/25 ($25k per person, $50k per accident bodily injury, $25k property damage). State minimums vary widely.
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Personal Auto Policy (PAP) > Liability Coverage

Name: Bodily Injury Liability
Plain-English Description: Pays for injuries you cause to other people, including medical costs, lost wages and legal claims.
Example: A driver who injures a pedestrian has the victim's bills paid by the policy.
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Personal Auto Policy (PAP) > Liability Coverage > Bodily Injury Liability

Name: Property Damage Liability
Plain-English Description: Pays for damage you cause to other people's property, such as cars, fences or buildings.
Example: A driver hits a mailbox and a parked car, and both are paid for.
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Personal Auto Policy (PAP) > Liability Coverage > Property Damage Liability

Name: Combined Single Limit (CSL)
Plain-English Description: One total limit per accident that covers both bodily injury and property damage.
Example: A policy has a $300,000 combined limit instead of split limits.
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Personal Auto Policy (PAP) > Liability Coverage > Combined Single Limit (CSL)

Name: SR-22 / FR-44 Filings
Plain-English Description: A form an insurer files with the state to prove a high-risk driver carries required liability cover.
Example: After a DUI, a driver's insurer files an SR-22 for 3 years.
US Notes: FR-44 (higher limits) is used in Florida and Virginia after DUIs.
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Personal Auto Policy (PAP) > Liability Coverage > SR-22 / FR-44 Filings

Name: Physical Damage Coverage
Plain-English Description: Covers damage to your own vehicle. Lenders and lessors require it.
Example: A new car owner with a loan buys collision and comprehensive as the lender requires.
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Personal Auto Policy (PAP) > Physical Damage Coverage

Name: Collision Coverage
Plain-English Description: Pays for damage to your car from hitting another vehicle or object, regardless of fault.
Example: A driver slides into a guardrail on ice and collision pays for repairs.
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Personal Auto Policy (PAP) > Physical Damage Coverage > Collision Coverage

Name: Comprehensive (Other Than Collision)
Plain-English Description: Pays for damage to your car from non-crash events such as theft, hail, fire, flood, vandalism or hitting an animal.
Example: Hail dents a car's roof and the policy pays.
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Personal Auto Policy (PAP) > Physical Damage Coverage > Comprehensive (Other Than Collision)

Name: Full Glass Coverage
Plain-English Description: Pays to repair or replace windshields and windows with no deductible.
Example: A cracked windshield is replaced at no cost.
US Notes: Required to be offered with no deductible in some states (e.g. Florida, Kentucky, South Carolina).
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Personal Auto Policy (PAP) > Physical Damage Coverage > Full Glass Coverage

Name: First-Party Injury Coverages
Plain-English Description: Pays medical costs for you and your passengers, regardless of who caused the crash.
Example: A driver's own policy pays for her hospital visit after a crash.
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Personal Auto Policy (PAP) > First-Party Injury Coverages

Name: Personal Injury Protection (PIP)
Plain-English Description: Pays your medical bills, lost wages and other costs after a crash no matter who caused it.
Example: A Michigan driver's PIP pays his medical bills after a crash.
US Notes: Required in no-fault states such as FL, MI, NY, NJ, PA, MA, MN, HI, KS, KY, ND, UT. NJ, PA and KY let drivers choose limited or full tort options.
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Personal Auto Policy (PAP) > First-Party Injury Coverages > Personal Injury Protection (PIP)

Name: Medical Payments Coverage (MedPay)
Plain-English Description: Pays medical bills for you and passengers regardless of fault; narrower than PIP.
Example: A passenger's ambulance ride is covered.
US Notes: Optional in most states.
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Personal Auto Policy (PAP) > First-Party Injury Coverages > Medical Payments Coverage (MedPay)

Name: Uninsured / Underinsured Motorist (UM/UIM)
Plain-English Description: Pays for your injuries (and in some states car damage) if the at-fault driver has no insurance or too little.
Example: A hit-and-run driver injures you and your UM cover pays.
US Notes: Required in about 20 states and must be offered (rejectable in writing) in most others.
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Personal Auto Policy (PAP) > First-Party Injury Coverages > Uninsured / Underinsured Motorist (UM/UIM)

Name: Auto Endorsements & Add-Ons
Plain-English Description: Optional extras added to a car policy.
Example: A driver adds rental reimbursement and roadside assistance.
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Personal Auto Policy (PAP) > Auto Endorsements & Add-Ons

Name: GAP Insurance
Plain-English Description: Covers the difference between what you owe on a car loan or lease and the car's value if it is totaled.
Example: A new car is totaled six months after purchase and GAP covers the loan shortfall.
US Notes: Sold by insurers or as a dealer waiver; a few states limit dealer GAP.
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Personal Auto Policy (PAP) > Auto Endorsements & Add-Ons > GAP Insurance

Name: New Car Replacement
Plain-English Description: Replaces a totaled new car with a brand-new one of the same model rather than paying its depreciated value.
Example: A 1-year-old car is totaled and replaced with a new one.
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Personal Auto Policy (PAP) > Auto Endorsements & Add-Ons > New Car Replacement

Name: Rental Reimbursement
Plain-English Description: Pays for a rental car while yours is being repaired after a covered claim.
Example: A driver gets a rental car for 10 days during repairs.
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Personal Auto Policy (PAP) > Auto Endorsements & Add-Ons > Rental Reimbursement

Name: Roadside Assistance
Plain-English Description: Helps with towing, flat tires, dead batteries and lock-outs.
Example: A car breaks down on a highway and is towed to a garage.
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Personal Auto Policy (PAP) > Auto Endorsements & Add-Ons > Roadside Assistance

Name: Accident Forgiveness
Plain-English Description: Prevents your premium from rising after your first at-fault accident.
Example: A driver's rate doesn't rise after a minor fender-bender.
US Notes: Not permitted or restricted in some states (e.g. California).
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Personal Auto Policy (PAP) > Auto Endorsements & Add-Ons > Accident Forgiveness

Name: Custom Parts & Equipment
Plain-English Description: Covers aftermarket add-ons such as custom wheels or stereos.
Example: A stolen custom sound system is replaced.
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Personal Auto Policy (PAP) > Auto Endorsements & Add-Ons > Custom Parts & Equipment

Name: Rideshare Endorsement
Plain-English Description: Fills the gap in a personal policy when you drive for Uber, Lyft or delivery apps with the app on but no ride accepted.
Example: An Uber driver waiting for a ride request is covered after a crash.
US Notes: Most states have TNC laws setting required coverage by driving period.
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Personal Auto Policy (PAP) > Auto Endorsements & Add-Ons > Rideshare Endorsement

Name: Usage-Based Insurance (UBI)
Plain-English Description: Premiums based on how much or how well you drive, measured by an app or plug-in device.
Example: A careful driver uses an insurer app to earn a discount.
US Notes: Examples: Progressive Snapshot, State Farm Drive Safe & Save, Allstate Milewise (pay-per-mile).
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Personal Auto Policy (PAP) > Usage-Based Insurance (UBI)

Name: Non-Standard Auto
Plain-English Description: Auto insurance for drivers with poor records, lapses in cover or no credit history.
Example: A driver with two speeding tickets and a lapse buys non-standard cover.
US Notes: Drivers who can't find cover can use state auto insurance plans (assigned risk).
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Personal Auto Policy (PAP) > Non-Standard Auto

Name: Non-Owner Car Insurance
Plain-English Description: Liability cover for people who drive but don't own a car.
Example: A city resident who rents cars often buys a non-owner policy.
US Notes: Often used to satisfy an SR-22 requirement.
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Personal Auto Policy (PAP) > Non-Owner Car Insurance

Name: Classic / Collector Car
Plain-English Description: Covers vintage and collector cars at an agreed value, usually with mileage and storage rules.
Example: A 1967 Mustang owner insures the car for its agreed value of $60,000.
US Notes: Specialist carriers include Hagerty and Grundy.
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Personal Auto Policy (PAP) > Classic / Collector Car

Name: Motorcycle Insurance
Plain-English Description: Cover for motorcycles, scooters and mopeds, with liability, physical damage and injury options similar to cars.
Example: A rider insures a Harley-Davidson.
US Notes: Required in almost every state; helmet laws vary.
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Motorcycle Insurance

Name: Recreational Vehicles
Plain-English Description: Cover for motorhomes, trailers, ATVs, snowmobiles and golf carts.
Example: A family insures its travel trailer.
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Recreational Vehicles

Name: RV / Motorhome
Plain-English Description: Covers motorhomes and travel trailers, including contents and vacation liability.
Example: A retired couple insures their RV for a cross-country trip.
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Recreational Vehicles > RV / Motorhome

Name: ATV / Off-Road Vehicle
Plain-English Description: Covers ATVs, UTVs and dirt bikes.
Example: An ATV rolls over on a trail and repairs are paid.
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Recreational Vehicles > ATV / Off-Road Vehicle

Name: Snowmobile
Plain-English Description: Covers snowmobiles and their riders' liability.
Example: A snowmobiler hits a fence and liability pays.
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Recreational Vehicles > Snowmobile

Name: Commercial Auto
Plain-English Description: Cover for vehicles used for business, such as vans, trucks, delivery vehicles and limos.
Example: A plumbing company insures its five vans.
US Notes: Based on the ISO Business Auto Policy (BAP). Federal FMCSA minimum limits apply to interstate carriers ($750,000+ for general freight).
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Commercial Auto

Name: Business Auto Policy (BAP)
Plain-English Description: Covers company-owned cars, vans and light trucks.
Example: A landscaping company insures its pickup trucks.
US Notes: Uses covered auto symbols (1-9) to define which vehicles are covered.
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Commercial Auto > Business Auto Policy (BAP)

Name: Hired & Non-Owned Auto (HNOA)
Plain-English Description: Covers a business's liability when employees drive rented cars or their own cars for work.
Example: An employee crashes their own car on a sales trip and the company is sued.
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Commercial Auto > Hired & Non-Owned Auto (HNOA)

Name: Trucking Insurance
Plain-English Description: Cover for businesses that haul goods for others.
Example: A regional carrier insures 40 tractor-trailers.
US Notes: Interstate for-hire carriers file proof of insurance with FMCSA (MCS-90 endorsement).
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Commercial Auto > Trucking Insurance

Name: Primary Auto Liability
Plain-English Description: The main liability cover for a truck fleet, meeting federal minimums.
Example: A carrier carries $1 million primary liability.
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Commercial Auto > Trucking Insurance > Primary Auto Liability

Name: Motor Truck Cargo
Plain-English Description: Covers goods being carried in a truck against loss or damage.
Example: A trucker's load of TVs is stolen and cargo cover pays.
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Commercial Auto > Trucking Insurance > Motor Truck Cargo

Name: Truck Physical Damage
Plain-English Description: Covers damage to trucks and trailers.
Example: A truck damaged in a rollover is repaired.
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Commercial Auto > Trucking Insurance > Truck Physical Damage

Name: Non-Trucking Liability / Bobtail
Plain-English Description: Covers owner-operators driving a truck when not under dispatch for a motor carrier.
Example: An owner-operator driving home without a trailer is covered.
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Commercial Auto > Trucking Insurance > Non-Trucking Liability / Bobtail

Name: Garage & Dealers
Plain-English Description: Covers auto dealers, repair shops and parking operators for their operations and customers' vehicles.
Example: A mechanic's customer car is damaged during a test drive.
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Commercial Auto > Garage & Dealers

Name: Garagekeepers Coverage
Plain-English Description: Covers customers' vehicles in your care, custody and control.
Example: A fire in a repair shop damages five customer cars.
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Commercial Auto > Garage & Dealers > Garagekeepers Coverage

Name: Dealers Open Lot
Plain-English Description: Covers a dealer's inventory of vehicles on the lot.
Example: A hailstorm damages 50 new cars on a dealer's lot.
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Commercial Auto > Garage & Dealers > Dealers Open Lot

Name: Public Auto / Livery
Plain-English Description: Covers taxis, limos, buses and other vehicles carrying paying passengers.
Example: A limousine company insures its fleet with higher limits.
US Notes: Required limits often set by city or state regulators.
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Commercial Auto > Public Auto / Livery

Name: TNC Commercial Policy
Plain-English Description: Policies bought by rideshare companies like Uber and Lyft covering drivers once a ride is accepted.
Example: A crash during an Uber ride is covered by Uber's insurer.
US Notes: State TNC laws typically require $1 million liability while a passenger is on board.
Full Path: Auto Insurance > Commercial Auto > TNC Commercial Policy

Name: Commercial Lines (Business Property & Packages)
Plain-English Description: Insurance businesses buy to protect their buildings, equipment, income and operations. Business liability, workers' comp and commercial auto are in their own branches.
Example: A bakery buys cover for its ovens, premises and lost income after a fire.
US Notes: Most standard commercial forms come from ISO. Larger or unusual risks often go to the excess and surplus (E&S) lines market, which has lighter rate and form regulation.
Full Path: Commercial Lines (Business Property & Packages)

Name: Business Package Policies
Plain-English Description: Bundles of common business covers sold as one policy.
Example: A dental office buys one package for building, contents and liability.
Full Path: Commercial Lines (Business Property & Packages) > Business Package Policies

Name: Business Owner's Policy (BOP)
Plain-English Description: A package for small and mid-sized businesses combining property, business income and general liability.
Example: A small retail shop buys a BOP for about $1,000 a year.
US Notes: Eligibility limited by size and class (e.g. offices, retail, restaurants, contractors).
Full Path: Commercial Lines (Business Property & Packages) > Business Package Policies > Business Owner's Policy (BOP)

Name: Commercial Package Policy (CPP)
Plain-English Description: A package for larger businesses built from separate ISO coverage parts (property, GL, crime, inland marine, equipment breakdown).
Example: A mid-size manufacturer builds a CPP with property, GL and crime.
US Notes: Qualifies for a package discount when property and GL are combined.
Full Path: Commercial Lines (Business Property & Packages) > Business Package Policies > Commercial Package Policy (CPP)

Name: Industry Program Policies
Plain-English Description: Tailored packages for a specific industry, often written through program administrators or MGAs.
Example: A chain of fitness studios buys a fitness-industry package.
Full Path: Commercial Lines (Business Property & Packages) > Business Package Policies > Industry Program Policies

Name: Commercial Property
Also Known As: Business property; Building and personal property
Plain-English Description: Covers business buildings, equipment, inventory and improvements against fire, storm and other damage.
Example: A warehouse fire destroys inventory and the insurer pays to replace it.
US Notes: ISO Building and Personal Property Coverage Form (CP 00 10).
Full Path: Commercial Lines (Business Property & Packages) > Commercial Property

Name: Causes of Loss Forms
Plain-English Description: ISO forms that define which perils are covered.
Example: A business picks the special form for the broadest cover.
Full Path: Commercial Lines (Business Property & Packages) > Commercial Property > Causes of Loss Forms

Name: Basic Form
Plain-English Description: A short named-peril list such as fire, lightning, explosion, windstorm, smoke, riot and vandalism.
Example: A low-budget policy for a vacant building.
Full Path: Commercial Lines (Business Property & Packages) > Commercial Property > Causes of Loss Forms > Basic Form

Name: Broad Form
Plain-English Description: Adds falling objects, weight of snow and water damage to the basic list.
Example: A business picks broad form for more named perils.
Full Path: Commercial Lines (Business Property & Packages) > Commercial Property > Causes of Loss Forms > Broad Form

Name: Special Form
Plain-English Description: Covers all causes of loss except those excluded.
Example: Most commercial property is written on the special form.
Full Path: Commercial Lines (Business Property & Packages) > Commercial Property > Causes of Loss Forms > Special Form

Name: Blanket Coverage
Plain-English Description: One limit applies across several buildings or locations rather than separate limits for each.
Example: A retailer with 10 stores uses a blanket limit.
Full Path: Commercial Lines (Business Property & Packages) > Commercial Property > Blanket Coverage

Name: Difference in Conditions (DIC)
Plain-English Description: Fills gaps in a main property policy, usually adding earthquake and flood.
Example: A California office building buys DIC for earthquake.
Full Path: Commercial Lines (Business Property & Packages) > Commercial Property > Difference in Conditions (DIC)

Name: Commercial Glass
Plain-English Description: Covers breakage of storefront windows and glass fittings.
Example: A shop's front window is smashed by vandals.
Full Path: Commercial Lines (Business Property & Packages) > Commercial Property > Commercial Glass

Name: Spoilage Coverage
Plain-English Description: Covers perishable stock that spoils after power failure or refrigeration breakdown.
Example: A grocer's frozen food spoils when a freezer fails.
Full Path: Commercial Lines (Business Property & Packages) > Commercial Property > Spoilage Coverage

Name: Terrorism Coverage (TRIA)
Plain-English Description: Covers damage from certified acts of terrorism, backed by a federal reinsurance program.
Example: An office tower buys terrorism cover.
US Notes: The Terrorism Risk Insurance Act requires insurers to offer the cover; the federal backstop runs through 2027 under current law.
Full Path: Commercial Lines (Business Property & Packages) > Commercial Property > Terrorism Coverage (TRIA)

Name: Business Income & Extra Expense
Plain-English Description: Pays lost profit and continuing expenses when a business can't operate after physical damage from a covered cause.
Example: A restaurant closed for 3 months after a fire receives its lost profits.
US Notes: ISO form CP 00 30.
Full Path: Commercial Lines (Business Property & Packages) > Business Income & Extra Expense

Name: Extra Expense
Plain-English Description: Pays extra costs to keep running after damage, such as renting temporary space.
Example: An office rents a temporary floor while its own is repaired.
Full Path: Commercial Lines (Business Property & Packages) > Business Income & Extra Expense > Extra Expense

Name: Contingent Business Income
Plain-English Description: Covers lost income when a key supplier or customer suffers covered damage.
Example: A car maker loses income when a parts supplier's factory burns.
Full Path: Commercial Lines (Business Property & Packages) > Business Income & Extra Expense > Contingent Business Income

Name: Civil Authority
Plain-English Description: Covers lost income when authorities prohibit access to your premises because of nearby damage.
Example: Police close a street after an explosion next door.
US Notes: Heavily litigated after COVID-19 closures; courts mostly found no physical loss.
Full Path: Commercial Lines (Business Property & Packages) > Business Income & Extra Expense > Civil Authority

Name: Utility Services - Time Element
Plain-English Description: Covers lost income when an off-site utility (power, water, telecom) fails due to covered damage.
Example: A power station fire shuts down a factory for 4 days.
Full Path: Commercial Lines (Business Property & Packages) > Business Income & Extra Expense > Utility Services - Time Element

Name: Builder's Risk
Plain-English Description: Covers buildings under construction or renovation, including materials on site.
Example: A developer insures a new apartment block during construction.
US Notes: Often written as inland marine in the US.
Full Path: Commercial Lines (Business Property & Packages) > Builder's Risk

Name: Wrap-Up Programs (OCIP / CCIP)
Plain-English Description: One insurance program bought by the owner (OCIP) or general contractor (CCIP) covering all contractors on a large project.
Example: A stadium project buys an OCIP covering GL and workers' comp for all trades.
US Notes: Some states restrict wrap-ups on public projects.
Full Path: Commercial Lines (Business Property & Packages) > Builder's Risk > Wrap-Up Programs (OCIP / CCIP)

Name: Soft Costs / Delay in Completion
Plain-English Description: Covers extra interest, fees and lost rent when a project is delayed by covered damage.
Example: A storm delays an apartment building's opening by 3 months.
Full Path: Commercial Lines (Business Property & Packages) > Builder's Risk > Soft Costs / Delay in Completion

Name: Equipment Breakdown
Plain-English Description: Covers sudden mechanical or electrical breakdown of equipment like boilers, HVAC and computers, which property policies exclude.
Example: A restaurant's walk-in cooler compressor burns out.
US Notes: Many states require boiler inspections, often performed by the equipment breakdown insurer.
Full Path: Commercial Lines (Business Property & Packages) > Equipment Breakdown

Name: Farm & Ranch Property
Plain-English Description: Package cover for farm dwellings, barns, equipment and livestock plus farm liability.
Example: A dairy farm insures its barns and milking equipment.
US Notes: Crop insurance is separate (see Agricultural). ISO and AAIS publish farm forms.
Full Path: Commercial Lines (Business Property & Packages) > Farm & Ranch Property

Name: Habitational & Real Estate
Plain-English Description: Property and liability for landlords, apartment complexes and HOAs.
Example: An apartment owner insures a 200-unit complex.
Full Path: Commercial Lines (Business Property & Packages) > Habitational & Real Estate

Name: Condo / HOA Master Policy
Plain-English Description: Covers a condo or HOA's common property, buildings and liability.
Example: An HOA insures the building shell, lobby and pool.
US Notes: Coverage scope ("bare walls" vs "all-in") depends on state law and association documents.
Full Path: Commercial Lines (Business Property & Packages) > Habitational & Real Estate > Condo / HOA Master Policy

Name: Lessor's Risk Only (LRO)
Plain-English Description: Covers a landlord's building and liability when the whole building is leased to tenants.
Example: An owner of a leased strip mall buys LRO.
Full Path: Commercial Lines (Business Property & Packages) > Habitational & Real Estate > Lessor's Risk Only (LRO)

Name: Vacant Building
Plain-English Description: Cover for buildings that are vacant or unoccupied, which standard policies restrict.
Example: A bank insures a foreclosed commercial building.
US Notes: Standard forms limit cover after 60 days of vacancy.
Full Path: Commercial Lines (Business Property & Packages) > Habitational & Real Estate > Vacant Building

Name: Marine, Aviation & Transit
Plain-English Description: Covers ships, aircraft, satellites and goods while moving, plus related liabilities. In the US, marine is split into ocean marine and inland marine.
Example: A coffee importer insures a container shipment from Brazil to New Jersey.
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit

Name: Ocean Marine
Plain-English Description: Covers vessels, cargo and liabilities connected with shipping by water.
Example: A shipping line insures its vessels and the cargo they carry.
US Notes: Governed by federal admiralty (maritime) law as well as state insurance rules.
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit > Ocean Marine

Name: Ocean Cargo
Plain-English Description: Covers goods shipped by sea (and connecting land or air legs) against loss or damage.
Example: Electronics damaged by seawater in transit are paid for.
US Notes: Carrier liability under COGSA is limited to $500 per package, so shippers buy cargo insurance.
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit > Ocean Marine > Ocean Cargo

Name: All Risks Cargo
Plain-English Description: The broadest cargo terms: covers all physical loss or damage except listed exclusions like poor packing and delay.
Example: A high-value machinery shipment is insured on all-risks terms.
US Notes: Based on American Institute Cargo Clauses.
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit > Ocean Marine > Ocean Cargo > All Risks Cargo

Name: With Average (WA)
Plain-English Description: Named-peril cover that pays partial losses from perils like heavy weather once they exceed a small threshold.
Example: Bulk steel is insured on WA terms.
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit > Ocean Marine > Ocean Cargo > With Average (WA)

Name: Free of Particular Average (FPA)
Plain-English Description: The narrowest terms: pays total losses and partial losses only from major casualties like sinking, fire or collision.
Example: Low-value bulk goods are insured FPA.
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit > Ocean Marine > Ocean Cargo > Free of Particular Average (FPA)

Name: Open Cargo Policy
Plain-English Description: Automatically covers all shipments over time under agreed terms, with each shipment reported.
Example: An importer reports each shipment under an annual open policy.
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit > Ocean Marine > Ocean Cargo > Open Cargo Policy

Name: Stock Throughput (STP)
Plain-English Description: Covers goods from raw material through storage and transit to final delivery in one policy.
Example: A retailer's stock is covered from supplier warehouse to store shelf.
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit > Ocean Marine > Ocean Cargo > Stock Throughput (STP)

Name: Hull & Machinery (H&M)
Plain-English Description: Covers physical damage to the ship itself and its machinery.
Example: A tanker's hull is repaired after a grounding.
US Notes: Often written on American Institute Hull Clauses.
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit > Ocean Marine > Hull & Machinery (H&M)

Name: Blue-Water Hull
Plain-English Description: Hull cover for ocean-going ships.
Example: A container ship owner insures its fleet.
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit > Ocean Marine > Hull & Machinery (H&M) > Blue-Water Hull

Name: Brown-Water Hull
Plain-English Description: Hull cover for barges, tugs and towboats on rivers and coastal waters.
Example: A Mississippi River towboat operator insures its fleet.
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit > Ocean Marine > Hull & Machinery (H&M) > Brown-Water Hull

Name: Marine War Risks
Plain-English Description: Covers ships and cargo against war, strikes, terrorism and piracy excluded by standard hull and cargo terms.
Example: A ship passing through a conflict zone buys extra war cover.
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit > Ocean Marine > Hull & Machinery (H&M) > Marine War Risks

Name: Shipbuilders' Risk
Plain-English Description: Covers ships while being built or repaired at a shipyard.
Example: A shipyard insures a ferry under construction.
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit > Ocean Marine > Hull & Machinery (H&M) > Shipbuilders' Risk

Name: Marine Liability
Plain-English Description: Covers liabilities from vessel operations and waterfront businesses.
Example: A shipowner is liable for an oil spill.
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit > Ocean Marine > Marine Liability

Name: Protection & Indemnity (P&I)
Plain-English Description: Covers shipowners' third-party liabilities such as crew injury, cargo damage, pollution and wreck removal, often through mutual P&I clubs.
Example: A shipowner's P&I pays for cleaning up a fuel spill.
US Notes: Vessels in US waters must show financial responsibility under the Oil Pollution Act of 1990 (OPA 90).
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit > Ocean Marine > Marine Liability > Protection & Indemnity (P&I)

Name: Maritime Employers Liability (MEL)
Plain-English Description: Covers employers of seamen for injury claims under the Jones Act and general maritime law.
Example: A deckhand injured on a crew boat sues his employer.
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit > Ocean Marine > Marine Liability > Maritime Employers Liability (MEL)

Name: Charterer's Liability
Plain-English Description: Covers companies that charter ships against liabilities to the owner and others.
Example: A charterer loads an unsafe cargo that damages the ship.
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit > Ocean Marine > Marine Liability > Charterer's Liability

Name: Marine Terminal Operators Liability
Plain-English Description: Covers port and terminal operators against damage to ships, cargo and people.
Example: A terminal crane drops a container onto a ship.
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit > Ocean Marine > Marine Liability > Marine Terminal Operators Liability

Name: Ship Repairers Liability
Plain-English Description: Covers shipyards for damage to vessels in their care.
Example: A vessel catches fire while in dry dock.
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit > Ocean Marine > Marine Liability > Ship Repairers Liability

Name: Yacht & Boat Insurance
Plain-English Description: Covers private boats and yachts for damage, theft and liability.
Example: A sailor insures a 40-foot yacht.
US Notes: Marinas and lenders usually require liability cover. Some states (e.g. Utah) require boat liability insurance.
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit > Ocean Marine > Yacht & Boat Insurance

Name: Inland Marine
Plain-English Description: A US-specific class covering property in transit over land, movable property, and "instrumentalities of transportation" such as bridges and pipelines.
Example: A contractor insures tools that move between job sites.
US Notes: Defined by the NAIC Nationwide Marine Definition; many inland marine forms are unfiled, giving flexibility.
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit > Inland Marine

Name: Contractor's Equipment Floater
Plain-English Description: Covers mobile construction equipment wherever it is.
Example: A stolen skid-steer loader is replaced.
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit > Inland Marine > Contractor's Equipment Floater

Name: Installation Floater
Plain-English Description: Covers materials being installed at a job site until the job is accepted.
Example: HVAC units awaiting installation are stolen from a site.
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit > Inland Marine > Installation Floater

Name: Transit Coverage
Plain-English Description: Covers the insured's own goods while transported by its own trucks or by carriers.
Example: A manufacturer's goods are damaged on its own truck.
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit > Inland Marine > Transit Coverage

Name: Bailee's Customers
Plain-English Description: Covers customers' property held by a business, such as a dry cleaner or repair shop.
Example: A fire at a dry cleaner destroys customers' clothes.
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit > Inland Marine > Bailee's Customers

Name: Electronic Data Processing (EDP)
Plain-English Description: Covers computers, servers and media, including breakdown and data restoration.
Example: A power surge fries a firm's servers.
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit > Inland Marine > Electronic Data Processing (EDP)

Name: Accounts Receivable
Plain-English Description: Pays amounts you can't collect because records of who owes you were destroyed.
Example: A fire destroys billing records and unpaid invoices are covered.
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit > Inland Marine > Accounts Receivable

Name: Valuable Papers & Records
Plain-English Description: Pays to restore important documents like blueprints and legal papers.
Example: An architect's plans are destroyed in a flood.
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit > Inland Marine > Valuable Papers & Records

Name: Jewelers Block
Plain-English Description: Open-peril cover for jewelry retailers' and wholesalers' stock, including customers' items.
Example: A jewelry store's safe is burglarized.
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit > Inland Marine > Jewelers Block

Name: Fine Arts (Commercial)
Plain-English Description: Covers artworks owned or held by galleries, museums and dealers, including in transit.
Example: A painting lent to a museum is damaged in transit.
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit > Inland Marine > Fine Arts (Commercial)

Name: Signs Coverage
Plain-English Description: Covers outdoor signs against damage.
Example: A storm destroys a restaurant's roadside sign.
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit > Inland Marine > Signs Coverage

Name: Instrumentalities of Transportation
Plain-English Description: Covers fixed property used in transportation and communication, such as bridges, tunnels, pipelines and cell towers.
Example: A toll bridge authority insures its bridge.
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit > Inland Marine > Instrumentalities of Transportation

Name: Aviation Insurance
Plain-English Description: Covers aircraft, airports and aviation businesses against physical damage and liability.
Example: An airline insures its fleet against crashes and passenger claims.
US Notes: FAA and DOT set some financial responsibility rules (e.g. for air carriers).
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit > Aviation Insurance

Name: Aircraft Hull
Plain-English Description: Covers physical damage to the aircraft, on the ground or in flight.
Example: A plane damaged in a hard landing is repaired.
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit > Aviation Insurance > Aircraft Hull

Name: Aircraft Liability
Plain-English Description: Covers liability to passengers and people or property on the ground.
Example: An airline pays compensation to injured passengers.
US Notes: International flights are subject to the Montreal Convention liability rules.
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit > Aviation Insurance > Aircraft Liability

Name: Airport & Ground Handler Liability
Plain-English Description: Covers airports, FBOs and ground handlers against third-party claims.
Example: A baggage vehicle damages a parked aircraft.
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit > Aviation Insurance > Airport & Ground Handler Liability

Name: Aviation Products Liability
Plain-English Description: Covers manufacturers of aircraft and parts against liability for defects.
Example: A parts maker is sued after an engine component fails.
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit > Aviation Insurance > Aviation Products Liability

Name: General Aviation
Plain-English Description: Covers privately owned planes, flight schools and small charter operators.
Example: A private pilot insures a Cessna 172.
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit > Aviation Insurance > General Aviation

Name: Non-Owned Aircraft Liability
Plain-English Description: Covers pilots who rent or borrow aircraft.
Example: A student pilot renting a plane buys renter's cover.
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit > Aviation Insurance > Non-Owned Aircraft Liability

Name: Drone (UAS) Insurance
Plain-English Description: Covers drones against damage and liability to others.
Example: A real estate photographer insures a camera drone.
US Notes: Commercial drone pilots need FAA Part 107 certification; insurance is not federally required but is often required by clients.
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit > Aviation Insurance > Drone (UAS) Insurance

Name: Space Insurance
Plain-English Description: Covers satellites and launch vehicles during launch and in orbit, plus third-party liability.
Example: A telecom company insures a satellite launch.
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit > Space Insurance

Name: Launch Insurance
Plain-English Description: Covers loss or failure of a satellite during launch and early operation.
Example: A rocket failure destroys a satellite and the insurer pays.
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit > Space Insurance > Launch Insurance

Name: In-Orbit Insurance
Plain-English Description: Covers satellites against failure once operating in space.
Example: A satellite's solar panel fails and lost capacity is paid.
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit > Space Insurance > In-Orbit Insurance

Name: Launch Third-Party Liability
Plain-English Description: Covers damage caused by launches to people and property on the ground.
Example: A launch operator buys liability cover required for its license.
US Notes: FAA licensing requires "maximum probable loss" liability cover, with a federal indemnification backstop above it under the Commercial Space Launch Act.
Full Path: Marine, Aviation & Transit > Space Insurance > Launch Third-Party Liability

Name: Specialty Insurance
Plain-English Description: Covers unusual, complex or modern risks that standard policies exclude. Many are written in the excess and surplus (E&S) market or at Lloyd's.
Example: A tech firm buys cyber cover; a film studio insures a shoot.
US Notes: E&S (non-admitted) insurers can write risks admitted carriers decline; they aren't backed by state guaranty funds and buyers pay a surplus lines tax.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance

Name: Cyber Insurance
Plain-English Description: Covers losses and liabilities from data breaches, hacking, ransomware and IT failures.
Example: A clinic hit by ransomware gets help restoring systems and notifying patients.
US Notes: All 50 states have data breach notification laws; SEC rules (2023) require public companies to disclose material cyber incidents.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Cyber Insurance

Name: Cyber First-Party Coverage
Plain-English Description: Pays your own costs after a cyber incident.
Example: A retailer's costs to investigate a breach are paid.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Cyber Insurance > Cyber First-Party Coverage

Name: Breach Response & Forensics
Plain-English Description: Pays for forensic experts, breach lawyers, notification letters, credit monitoring and PR.
Example: Investigators find how hackers got in and customers are notified.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Cyber Insurance > Cyber First-Party Coverage > Breach Response & Forensics

Name: Cyber Extortion / Ransomware
Plain-English Description: Covers ransom demands (where legal) and negotiation costs.
Example: A firm's data is encrypted and negotiators are hired.
US Notes: Payments to sanctioned groups are barred by OFAC (Treasury) rules.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Cyber Insurance > Cyber First-Party Coverage > Cyber Extortion / Ransomware

Name: Network Business Interruption
Plain-English Description: Covers lost income while systems are down after an attack or, if included, a system failure.
Example: An online shop loses 3 days of sales during an attack.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Cyber Insurance > Cyber First-Party Coverage > Network Business Interruption

Name: Dependent (Contingent) Cyber BI
Plain-English Description: Covers lost income when a vendor or cloud provider you rely on suffers an outage or attack.
Example: A pharmacy chain loses sales when its claims processor is hacked.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Cyber Insurance > Cyber First-Party Coverage > Dependent (Contingent) Cyber BI

Name: Data Restoration
Plain-English Description: Pays to recover or recreate damaged data and software.
Example: A firm rebuilds its database after malware deletes it.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Cyber Insurance > Cyber First-Party Coverage > Data Restoration

Name: Social Engineering / Funds Transfer Fraud
Plain-English Description: Covers money lost when employees are tricked into wiring funds to criminals, such as in business email compromise.
Example: An accounts clerk pays a fake invoice from a spoofed vendor email.
US Notes: Often sub-limited; may also sit in a crime policy.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Cyber Insurance > Cyber First-Party Coverage > Social Engineering / Funds Transfer Fraud

Name: Cyber Third-Party Liability
Plain-English Description: Covers claims from others harmed by your cyber incident.
Example: Customers sue a company after their card details leak.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Cyber Insurance > Cyber Third-Party Liability

Name: Privacy & Network Security Liability
Plain-English Description: Covers lawsuits for failing to protect data or for passing malware to others.
Example: Patients whose records leaked file a class action.
US Notes: Exposure driven by laws like HIPAA, CCPA/CPRA (California) and BIPA (Illinois biometrics).
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Cyber Insurance > Cyber Third-Party Liability > Privacy & Network Security Liability

Name: Regulatory Defense & Penalties
Plain-English Description: Covers regulatory investigations and fines where insurable by law.
Example: A company is investigated by a state attorney general after a breach.
US Notes: Insurability of fines varies by state.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Cyber Insurance > Cyber Third-Party Liability > Regulatory Defense & Penalties

Name: Media Liability
Plain-English Description: Covers claims of defamation, privacy invasion or IP infringement from online content.
Example: A blog post leads to a defamation claim.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Cyber Insurance > Cyber Third-Party Liability > Media Liability

Name: PCI-DSS Fines & Assessments
Plain-English Description: Covers card brand fines and assessments after a payment card breach.
Example: A merchant is charged by card brands after a breach.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Cyber Insurance > Cyber Third-Party Liability > PCI-DSS Fines & Assessments

Name: Personal Cyber / Identity Theft
Plain-English Description: Covers individuals for identity restoration, online fraud and cyberbullying costs.
Example: A person's identity is stolen and the policy pays to restore credit.
US Notes: Often an endorsement to homeowners policies.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Cyber Insurance > Personal Cyber / Identity Theft

Name: Professional Liability (E&O)
Plain-English Description: Covers professionals when a client claims their advice or service was negligent and caused financial loss or injury.
Example: An accountant is sued after a tax filing mistake costs a client money.
US Notes: Usually written on a claims-made basis.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Professional Liability (E&O)

Name: Medical Malpractice
Plain-English Description: Covers doctors, nurses and hospitals against claims of negligent treatment.
Example: A surgeon is sued after a complication.
US Notes: Some states require it for licensure or patient compensation funds; many states cap non-economic damages.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Professional Liability (E&O) > Medical Malpractice

Name: Physicians & Surgeons
Plain-English Description: Individual or group cover for doctors.
Example: An OB-GYN buys cover with $1M/$3M limits.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Professional Liability (E&O) > Medical Malpractice > Physicians & Surgeons

Name: Hospital Professional Liability
Plain-English Description: Covers hospitals and health systems for patient care claims.
Example: A hospital is sued after a medication error.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Professional Liability (E&O) > Medical Malpractice > Hospital Professional Liability

Name: Allied Health / Nurses
Plain-English Description: Covers nurses, therapists, pharmacists and other health workers.
Example: A physical therapist is sued for a patient's injury.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Professional Liability (E&O) > Medical Malpractice > Allied Health / Nurses

Name: Tail Coverage (ERP)
Plain-English Description: Extends a claims-made policy's reporting window after it ends, such as when a doctor retires or changes jobs.
Example: A retiring doctor buys tail cover for claims filed later.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Professional Liability (E&O) > Medical Malpractice > Tail Coverage (ERP)

Name: Lawyers Professional Liability (LPL)
Plain-English Description: Covers lawyers against claims of negligent legal work.
Example: A lawyer misses a filing deadline and the client sues.
US Notes: Only Oregon (through the Oregon State Bar PLF, since 1978) and Idaho (since 2018) require private-practice lawyers to carry it. About half the states require lawyers to disclose whether they carry it, either to clients or on bar registration forms.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Professional Liability (E&O) > Lawyers Professional Liability (LPL)

Name: Architects & Engineers (A&E)
Plain-English Description: Covers design professionals against claims of design errors.
Example: An engineer's calculation error causes a building defect.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Professional Liability (E&O) > Architects & Engineers (A&E)

Name: Technology E&O
Plain-English Description: Covers IT and software companies when their product or service fails and causes a client financial loss. Often combined with cyber.
Example: A software bug causes a client's billing system to fail.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Professional Liability (E&O) > Technology E&O

Name: Accountants Professional Liability
Plain-English Description: Covers accountants and bookkeepers against claims of errors in audits, tax or advice.
Example: A CPA misses a deduction and the client is fined.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Professional Liability (E&O) > Accountants Professional Liability

Name: Financial Services E&O
Plain-English Description: Covers advisers, brokers and asset managers against claims of negligent advice.
Example: An adviser is sued for unsuitable investments.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Professional Liability (E&O) > Financial Services E&O

Name: Insurance Agents & Brokers E&O
Plain-English Description: Covers insurance agents against claims they arranged the wrong cover.
Example: A broker forgets to add flood cover and the client sues.
US Notes: Required by some states and many carriers for appointment.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Professional Liability (E&O) > Insurance Agents & Brokers E&O

Name: Real Estate E&O
Plain-English Description: Covers real estate agents, brokers and appraisers against claims of misrepresentation or errors.
Example: A buyer sues an agent for failing to disclose a known defect.
US Notes: Required for licensees in a number of states (e.g. Colorado, Iowa, Kentucky).
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Professional Liability (E&O) > Real Estate E&O

Name: Miscellaneous Professional Liability (MPL)
Plain-English Description: Covers other professionals such as consultants, marketers and HR advisers.
Example: A marketing agency is sued for a failed campaign.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Professional Liability (E&O) > Miscellaneous Professional Liability (MPL)

Name: Management Liability
Plain-English Description: Covers company leaders and the company against claims about how the business is run.
Example: A company buys D&O, EPL and fiduciary cover together.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Management Liability

Name: Directors & Officers (D&O)
Plain-English Description: Covers directors and officers personally, and often the company, against claims of wrongful acts in managing the company.
Example: Shareholders sue directors after the share price falls.
US Notes: Delaware and other state corporate laws govern indemnification of directors.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Management Liability > Directors & Officers (D&O)

Name: Side A
Plain-English Description: Covers directors personally when the company can't or won't indemnify them, such as in bankruptcy.
Example: A director's defense costs are paid after the company goes bankrupt.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Management Liability > Directors & Officers (D&O) > Side A

Name: Side B
Plain-English Description: Reimburses the company for costs it pays to defend its directors.
Example: The company pays a director's legal fees and is reimbursed.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Management Liability > Directors & Officers (D&O) > Side B

Name: Side C
Plain-English Description: Covers the company itself, for securities claims (public companies) or broader claims (private companies).
Example: A listed company is sued in a securities class action.
US Notes: Securities class actions are brought under the Securities Act of 1933 and Exchange Act of 1934.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Management Liability > Directors & Officers (D&O) > Side C

Name: Public Company D&O
Plain-English Description: D&O for listed companies, focused on securities class actions and SEC investigations.
Example: A company's directors are sued after a missed earnings forecast.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Management Liability > Directors & Officers (D&O) > Public Company D&O

Name: Private Company & Nonprofit D&O
Plain-English Description: D&O for private companies and nonprofits, often bundled with EPL and fiduciary.
Example: A nonprofit board is sued by a donor.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Management Liability > Directors & Officers (D&O) > Private Company & Nonprofit D&O

Name: Employment Practices Liability (EPLI)
Plain-English Description: Covers claims from employees for wrongful termination, discrimination, harassment and retaliation.
Example: An ex-employee sues for wrongful termination.
US Notes: Claims arise under Title VII, ADA, ADEA and state laws; EEOC charges are a common trigger. Wage-and-hour claims are usually excluded.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Management Liability > Employment Practices Liability (EPLI)

Name: Fiduciary Liability
Plain-English Description: Covers people managing employee benefit plans (401(k), pension, health) against claims of mismanagement.
Example: Employees claim a 401(k) plan charged excessive fees.
US Notes: Fiduciary duties are imposed by ERISA; distinct from the ERISA fidelity bond.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Management Liability > Fiduciary Liability

Name: Kidnap, Ransom & Extortion (K&R)
Plain-English Description: Covers ransom payments, crisis consultants and related costs for kidnap, extortion and wrongful detention.
Example: A company's engineer is kidnapped abroad and crisis experts are sent.
US Notes: Paying ransom to sanctioned persons is prohibited by OFAC.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Kidnap, Ransom & Extortion (K&R)

Name: Political Risk Insurance (PRI)
Plain-English Description: Covers investors and lenders against losses caused by government actions or political violence abroad.
Example: A US company's mine in another country is seized by the government.
US Notes: Also available from the US International Development Finance Corporation (DFC).
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Political Risk Insurance (PRI)

Name: Confiscation, Expropriation & Nationalization (CEN)
Plain-English Description: Covers seizure of assets by a foreign government.
Example: A government nationalizes an oil field.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Political Risk Insurance (PRI) > Confiscation, Expropriation & Nationalization (CEN)

Name: Currency Inconvertibility & Transfer
Plain-English Description: Covers inability to convert local currency or move money out of a country.
Example: A company can't send profits home due to new currency controls.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Political Risk Insurance (PRI) > Currency Inconvertibility & Transfer

Name: Political Violence
Plain-English Description: Covers damage from war, riots, strikes and terrorism.
Example: A hotel abroad is damaged during civil unrest.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Political Risk Insurance (PRI) > Political Violence

Name: Contract Frustration
Plain-English Description: Covers losses when a foreign government buyer fails to pay or cancels a contract.
Example: A foreign ministry cancels a contract without paying.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Political Risk Insurance (PRI) > Contract Frustration

Name: Event & Entertainment Insurance
Plain-English Description: Covers events and productions against cancellation, damage and liability.
Example: A music festival is cancelled due to a storm.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Event & Entertainment Insurance

Name: Event Cancellation
Plain-English Description: Covers costs and lost income if an event is cancelled, postponed or relocated.
Example: A conference is cancelled when the venue floods.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Event & Entertainment Insurance > Event Cancellation

Name: Non-Appearance
Plain-English Description: Covers losses if a key performer or speaker can't appear.
Example: A headline singer falls ill before a concert.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Event & Entertainment Insurance > Non-Appearance

Name: Wedding / Special Event Insurance
Plain-English Description: Covers lost deposits and extra costs if a wedding is cancelled or goes wrong, plus event liability.
Example: A venue goes bankrupt and the wedding deposits are refunded.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Event & Entertainment Insurance > Wedding / Special Event Insurance

Name: Film & TV Production
Plain-English Description: Covers productions for equipment, cast illness, delays and liability.
Example: A lead actor's injury delays a film and costs are paid.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Event & Entertainment Insurance > Film & TV Production

Name: Prize Indemnity / Hole-in-One
Plain-English Description: Covers the cost of paying out a big prize in a promotion or contest.
Example: A golfer hits a hole-in-one and wins a car, paid by the insurer.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Event & Entertainment Insurance > Prize Indemnity / Hole-in-One

Name: Pet Insurance
Plain-English Description: Pays vet bills for pets' illnesses and injuries, usually by reimbursing you after you pay the vet.
Example: A dog's surgery for a torn ligament is reimbursed.
US Notes: The NAIC Pet Insurance Model Act (2022) has been adopted by a growing number of states.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Pet Insurance

Name: Accident-Only
Plain-English Description: Covers vet bills from accidents only, at a lower price.
Example: A cat hit by a car is treated.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Pet Insurance > Accident-Only

Name: Accident & Illness
Plain-English Description: Covers accidents and illnesses such as cancer, allergies and infections.
Example: A dog with diabetes has treatment paid every year.
US Notes: Pre-existing conditions are typically excluded.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Pet Insurance > Accident & Illness

Name: Wellness / Routine Care Add-On
Plain-English Description: Covers routine vaccinations, checkups and flea prevention.
Example: A puppy's vaccinations are covered.
US Notes: Wellness plans are not insurance under the NAIC model law.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Pet Insurance > Wellness / Routine Care Add-On

Name: Equine Insurance
Plain-English Description: Covers horses for death (equine mortality), major medical, surgery and liability.
Example: A horse owner's colic surgery bill is paid.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Pet Insurance > Equine Insurance

Name: Travel Insurance
Plain-English Description: Covers trip cancellations, medical emergencies abroad and lost luggage.
Example: A tourist breaks a leg in Italy and hospital costs are paid.
US Notes: Regulated by states; NAIC Travel Insurance Model Act adopted in many states. Medicare generally doesn't cover care abroad.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Travel Insurance

Name: Trip Cancellation & Interruption
Plain-English Description: Refunds prepaid, non-refundable costs if you must cancel or cut short a trip for a covered reason.
Example: A trip is cancelled due to a family death and costs are refunded.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Travel Insurance > Trip Cancellation & Interruption

Name: Cancel For Any Reason (CFAR)
Plain-English Description: Optional upgrade that refunds part of trip costs (often 50-75%) if you cancel for any reason.
Example: A traveler changes plans and gets 75% back.
US Notes: Must usually be bought within 14-21 days of first trip payment.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Travel Insurance > Cancel For Any Reason (CFAR)

Name: Travel Medical & Evacuation
Plain-English Description: Covers emergency medical treatment abroad and medical evacuation.
Example: A traveler is flown home after a stroke.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Travel Insurance > Travel Medical & Evacuation

Name: Baggage & Personal Effects
Plain-English Description: Covers lost, stolen or delayed luggage.
Example: Delayed bags lead to reimbursement for essentials.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Travel Insurance > Baggage & Personal Effects

Name: Annual Multi-Trip
Plain-English Description: Covers all trips in a year, each up to a maximum length.
Example: A consultant who travels monthly buys annual cover.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Travel Insurance > Annual Multi-Trip

Name: International Student Insurance
Plain-English Description: Health cover for foreign students studying in the US, often required by universities and J-1 visa rules.
Example: A J-1 exchange student buys a plan meeting State Department minimums.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Travel Insurance > International Student Insurance

Name: Extended Warranty / Service Contracts
Also Known As: Vehicle service contract; Mechanical breakdown insurance (MBI)
Plain-English Description: Covers repair of products or vehicles after the manufacturer's warranty ends.
Example: A washing machine breaks in year 3 and repairs are covered.
US Notes: Service contracts are regulated separately from insurance in most states; MBI is an insurance product sold by insurers (e.g. in California).
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Extended Warranty / Service Contracts

Name: Sports & Contingency
Plain-English Description: Specialist covers for athletes, teams and bloodstock.
Example: A team insures a player's salary during injury.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Sports & Contingency

Name: Athlete Permanent Total Disability
Plain-English Description: Pays athletes if an injury ends their career or reduces their draft value.
Example: A college football star insures future pro earnings.
US Notes: Some NCAA programs (Exceptional Student-Athlete Disability Insurance) help top athletes buy cover.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Sports & Contingency > Athlete Permanent Total Disability

Name: Bloodstock / Livestock Mortality
Plain-English Description: Covers death or injury of valuable racehorses and breeding animals.
Example: A Kentucky stud farm insures a stallion.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Sports & Contingency > Bloodstock / Livestock Mortality

Name: Transactional Risk Insurance
Plain-English Description: Covers risks in buying or selling a company.
Example: A buyer claims after discovering the target's accounts were wrong.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Transactional Risk Insurance

Name: Representations & Warranties (R&W)
Plain-English Description: Covers losses from breaches of the seller's promises in a purchase agreement.
Example: A buyer is paid when an undisclosed lawsuit emerges.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Transactional Risk Insurance > Representations & Warranties (R&W)

Name: Tax Liability Insurance
Plain-English Description: Covers the risk that the IRS or a state challenges a tax position.
Example: A deal's tax structure is challenged and extra tax is paid.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Transactional Risk Insurance > Tax Liability Insurance

Name: Contingent Risk / Judgment Preservation
Plain-English Description: Covers specific identified risks, such as losing a won judgment on appeal.
Example: A company insures its trial win against reversal.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Transactional Risk Insurance > Contingent Risk / Judgment Preservation

Name: Intellectual Property Insurance
Plain-English Description: Covers legal costs to defend against or enforce patents, trademarks and copyrights.
Example: A startup is sued by a patent assertion entity.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Intellectual Property Insurance

Name: Weather Insurance
Plain-English Description: Pays when weather such as rain, snow or temperature is worse than agreed; often parametric.
Example: An outdoor festival is paid if more than 0.5 inches of rain falls.
Full Path: Specialty Insurance > Weather Insurance

Name: Financial Lines
Plain-English Description: Insurance that protects against financial loss from non-payment, dishonesty, failed obligations or defects in ownership, rather than physical damage.
Example: A contractor gets a bond so a city will award it a road project.
Full Path: Financial Lines

Name: Credit Insurance
Plain-English Description: Protects lenders or sellers when borrowers or customers don't pay.
Example: A wholesaler is paid when a big customer goes bankrupt.
Full Path: Financial Lines > Credit Insurance

Name: Trade Credit Insurance
Plain-English Description: Protects a business when customers fail to pay invoices due to insolvency or long delays.
Example: A supplier is paid 90% of an unpaid invoice after a retailer goes bankrupt.
Full Path: Financial Lines > Credit Insurance > Trade Credit Insurance

Name: Whole Turnover Policy
Plain-English Description: Covers all of a business's credit sales to customers.
Example: A distributor insures all its receivables.
Full Path: Financial Lines > Credit Insurance > Trade Credit Insurance > Whole Turnover Policy

Name: Key Account / Single Buyer
Plain-English Description: Covers credit risk on one or a few major customers.
Example: A supplier insures its exposure to one large retailer.
Full Path: Financial Lines > Credit Insurance > Trade Credit Insurance > Key Account / Single Buyer

Name: Export Credit Insurance
Plain-English Description: Covers foreign buyers failing to pay, including political risks.
Example: A US exporter insures sales to a buyer abroad.
US Notes: Available from private insurers and the Export-Import Bank of the United States (EXIM).
Full Path: Financial Lines > Credit Insurance > Trade Credit Insurance > Export Credit Insurance

Name: Credit-Related Insurance (Consumer)
Plain-English Description: Pays a borrower's loan payments if they die, become disabled or lose their job.
Example: A car loan's payments are made while the borrower is disabled.
US Notes: Includes credit life, credit disability and involuntary unemployment; sales practices regulated by state consumer credit insurance laws.
Full Path: Financial Lines > Credit Insurance > Credit-Related Insurance (Consumer)

Name: Credit Disability
Plain-English Description: Makes loan payments while the borrower is disabled.
Example: A borrower's monthly car payment is covered during recovery from surgery.
Full Path: Financial Lines > Credit Insurance > Credit-Related Insurance (Consumer) > Credit Disability

Name: Involuntary Unemployment
Plain-English Description: Makes loan payments for a limited time after a job loss.
Example: A laid-off worker's credit card minimums are paid for 6 months.
Full Path: Financial Lines > Credit Insurance > Credit-Related Insurance (Consumer) > Involuntary Unemployment

Name: Creditor-Placed / Force-Placed Insurance
Plain-English Description: Insurance a lender buys and charges to the borrower when the borrower lets required cover lapse.
Example: A lender force-places hazard cover on a home after the owner's policy lapsed.
US Notes: Subject to CFPB (RESPA) rules for mortgages and state regulation.
Full Path: Financial Lines > Credit Insurance > Creditor-Placed / Force-Placed Insurance

Name: Mortgage Insurance
Plain-English Description: Protects a mortgage lender if the borrower defaults; the borrower usually pays for it.
Example: A buyer with a 10% down payment pays monthly mortgage insurance.
Full Path: Financial Lines > Mortgage Insurance

Name: Private Mortgage Insurance (PMI)
Plain-English Description: Required on conventional loans with less than 20% down; it can be cancelled once equity reaches 20% and must end automatically at 22%.
Example: A first-time buyer pays PMI until their loan-to-value falls to 80%.
US Notes: Cancellation rules set by the federal Homeowners Protection Act of 1998. Required by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac for high-LTV loans.
Full Path: Financial Lines > Mortgage Insurance > Private Mortgage Insurance (PMI)

Name: Borrower-Paid Monthly PMI
Plain-English Description: Premium added to the monthly mortgage payment.
Example: A buyer pays $120 a month in PMI.
Full Path: Financial Lines > Mortgage Insurance > Private Mortgage Insurance (PMI) > Borrower-Paid Monthly PMI

Name: Single-Premium PMI
Plain-English Description: PMI paid in one lump sum at closing.
Example: A buyer pays PMI upfront to lower monthly costs.
Full Path: Financial Lines > Mortgage Insurance > Private Mortgage Insurance (PMI) > Single-Premium PMI

Name: Lender-Paid Mortgage Insurance (LPMI)
Plain-English Description: The lender pays for PMI in exchange for a higher interest rate.
Example: A buyer accepts a slightly higher rate to avoid a separate PMI bill.
US Notes: Cannot be cancelled since it's built into the rate.
Full Path: Financial Lines > Mortgage Insurance > Private Mortgage Insurance (PMI) > Lender-Paid Mortgage Insurance (LPMI)

Name: FHA Mortgage Insurance Premium (MIP)
Plain-English Description: Government mortgage insurance on FHA loans, with an upfront premium and annual premium.
Example: A buyer with 3.5% down on an FHA loan pays MIP.
US Notes: Run by HUD's Federal Housing Administration; with less than 10% down, MIP lasts for the life of the loan.
Full Path: Financial Lines > Mortgage Insurance > FHA Mortgage Insurance Premium (MIP)

Name: VA Loan Guaranty
Plain-English Description: The Department of Veterans Affairs guarantees part of VA loans instead of mortgage insurance; borrowers pay a one-time funding fee.
Example: A veteran buys a home with 0% down.
US Notes: Federal program; certain disabled veterans are exempt from the fee.
Full Path: Financial Lines > Mortgage Insurance > VA Loan Guaranty

Name: USDA Loan Guarantee Fee
Plain-English Description: USDA guarantees rural home loans in exchange for upfront and annual fees.
Example: A family in a rural town buys a home with a USDA loan.
US Notes: USDA Rural Development program.
Full Path: Financial Lines > Mortgage Insurance > USDA Loan Guarantee Fee

Name: Title Insurance
Plain-English Description: Protects against losses from defects in the legal ownership of real estate, such as unknown liens, forged deeds or missing heirs. Paid once at closing.
Example: A buyer is protected when an unknown heir claims the house.
US Notes: Rates are promulgated by the state in some states (e.g. Texas, New Mexico); Iowa prohibits private title insurance and uses a state title guaranty division.
Full Path: Financial Lines > Title Insurance

Name: Owner's Title Policy
Plain-English Description: Protects the buyer's ownership stake for as long as they or their heirs own the property.
Example: A homeowner's title policy pays to defend against a forged deed claim.
US Notes: Optional in most states.
Full Path: Financial Lines > Title Insurance > Owner's Title Policy

Name: Lender's (Loan) Title Policy
Plain-English Description: Protects the lender's lien on the property up to the loan amount.
Example: A lender requires a loan policy before funding the mortgage.
US Notes: Required by virtually all mortgage lenders.
Full Path: Financial Lines > Title Insurance > Lender's (Loan) Title Policy

Name: ALTA Endorsements
Plain-English Description: Standard add-ons from the American Land Title Association covering specific issues like zoning, access or environmental liens.
Example: A commercial buyer adds a zoning endorsement.
US Notes: ALTA forms are used in most states; Texas and some others use their own forms.
Full Path: Financial Lines > Title Insurance > ALTA Endorsements

Name: Surety Bonds
Plain-English Description: A three-party guarantee: the surety promises the obligee (e.g. a project owner or government) that the principal (e.g. a contractor) will fulfil an obligation. Unlike insurance, the surety expects to be repaid by the principal for any loss.
Example: A builder's bond pays to finish a school when the builder goes bust.
US Notes: Federal construction projects over $150,000 require performance and payment bonds under the Miller Act; states have "Little Miller Acts".
Full Path: Financial Lines > Surety Bonds

Name: Contract Surety
Plain-English Description: Bonds guaranteeing construction contracts.
Example: A contractor bonds a highway project.
Full Path: Financial Lines > Surety Bonds > Contract Surety

Name: Bid Bond
Plain-English Description: Guarantees a contractor will sign the contract and provide bonds if it wins the bid.
Example: A contractor submits a 10% bid bond with its tender.
Full Path: Financial Lines > Surety Bonds > Contract Surety > Bid Bond

Name: Performance Bond
Plain-English Description: Guarantees the contractor will complete the project according to the contract.
Example: The surety hires a new contractor after the original one fails.
Full Path: Financial Lines > Surety Bonds > Contract Surety > Performance Bond

Name: Payment Bond
Plain-English Description: Guarantees subcontractors and suppliers will be paid.
Example: Unpaid subcontractors on a public project are paid by the surety.
Full Path: Financial Lines > Surety Bonds > Contract Surety > Payment Bond

Name: Maintenance / Warranty Bond
Plain-English Description: Guarantees defects found after completion will be fixed.
Example: A cracked road surface is repaired in year one.
Full Path: Financial Lines > Surety Bonds > Contract Surety > Maintenance / Warranty Bond

Name: Commercial Surety
Plain-English Description: Bonds required by laws, courts or contracts outside construction.
Example: A car dealer posts a bond to get a license.
Full Path: Financial Lines > Surety Bonds > Commercial Surety

Name: License & Permit Bonds
Plain-English Description: Required by states or cities before a business can get a license, guaranteeing it follows the law.
Example: A mortgage broker posts a state license bond.
Full Path: Financial Lines > Surety Bonds > Commercial Surety > License & Permit Bonds

Name: Court / Judicial Bonds
Plain-English Description: Required in legal proceedings, such as appeal bonds and bonds for estate executors.
Example: An executor posts a probate bond.
Full Path: Financial Lines > Surety Bonds > Commercial Surety > Court / Judicial Bonds

Name: Bail Bonds
Plain-English Description: Guarantees a defendant will appear in court; usually arranged by a bail bond agent for a non-refundable fee.
Example: A defendant's family pays a bail agent 10% of the bail amount.
US Notes: Commercial bail bonds are banned or restricted in some states (e.g. Illinois, Kentucky, Oregon, Wisconsin).
Full Path: Financial Lines > Surety Bonds > Commercial Surety > Bail Bonds

Name: Public Official Bonds
Plain-English Description: Guarantees elected or appointed officials will perform their duties honestly.
Example: A county treasurer is bonded.
Full Path: Financial Lines > Surety Bonds > Commercial Surety > Public Official Bonds

Name: Customs Bonds
Plain-English Description: Guarantees importers will pay duties and follow US Customs rules.
Example: An importer buys a continuous customs bond.
US Notes: Required by US Customs and Border Protection.
Full Path: Financial Lines > Surety Bonds > Commercial Surety > Customs Bonds

Name: Notary Bonds
Plain-English Description: Protects the public against a notary's errors or misconduct.
Example: A notary buys a bond required by the state.
US Notes: Required in many states.
Full Path: Financial Lines > Surety Bonds > Commercial Surety > Notary Bonds

Name: Fidelity & Crime
Plain-English Description: Protects a business from theft of money or property by employees or outsiders, including fraud and forgery.
Example: A bookkeeper embezzles $200,000 and the crime policy reimburses the company.
Full Path: Financial Lines > Fidelity & Crime

Name: Employee Theft
Plain-English Description: Covers theft of money, securities or property by employees.
Example: A warehouse manager steals inventory.
Full Path: Financial Lines > Fidelity & Crime > Employee Theft

Name: ERISA Fidelity Bond
Plain-English Description: A bond required for people who handle employee benefit plan money, protecting the plan against their theft.
Example: A 401(k) plan is bonded for 10% of its assets.
US Notes: Required by ERISA Section 412 (generally 10% of plan assets, up to $500,000 or $1 million for plans with employer securities).
Full Path: Financial Lines > Fidelity & Crime > ERISA Fidelity Bond

Name: Forgery or Alteration
Plain-English Description: Covers losses from forged or altered checks and similar documents.
Example: A forged company check is cashed.
Full Path: Financial Lines > Fidelity & Crime > Forgery or Alteration

Name: Computer & Funds Transfer Fraud
Plain-English Description: Covers theft through hacking into systems or fraudulent transfer instructions sent to your bank.
Example: A hacker instructs the bank to wire funds overseas.
Full Path: Financial Lines > Fidelity & Crime > Computer & Funds Transfer Fraud

Name: Third-Party (Client Property) Crime
Plain-English Description: Covers theft of a client's property by your employees.
Example: A janitorial worker steals from a client's office.
Full Path: Financial Lines > Fidelity & Crime > Third-Party (Client Property) Crime

Name: Business Service Bond
Plain-English Description: A bond small service firms buy to reassure clients against employee theft.
Example: A cleaning company advertises that it is bonded.
Full Path: Financial Lines > Fidelity & Crime > Business Service Bond

Name: Financial Institution Bond
Plain-English Description: Crime cover designed for banks, credit unions and brokerages.
Example: A bank teller's theft is covered.
US Notes: Standard forms from the Surety & Fidelity Association of America (SFAA). Credit unions must carry it under NCUA rules.
Full Path: Financial Lines > Fidelity & Crime > Financial Institution Bond

Name: Financial Guaranty Insurance
Plain-English Description: Guarantees timely payment of principal and interest on bonds if the issuer defaults.
Example: A city's school bonds are insured so they earn a higher credit rating.
US Notes: Written by monoline insurers (e.g. Assured Guaranty, Build America Mutual); New York Insurance Law Article 69 restricts it to monolines.
Full Path: Financial Lines > Financial Guaranty Insurance

Name: Agricultural & Crop Insurance
Plain-English Description: Protects farmers and ranchers against crop losses, falling revenue, livestock deaths and farm property damage.
Example: A corn farmer is paid when drought cuts the harvest in half.
US Notes: Most US crop insurance is the Federal Crop Insurance Program: sold and serviced by private Approved Insurance Providers, with premiums subsidized and reinsured by USDA's Risk Management Agency (RMA) through the Federal Crop Insurance Corporation (FCIC).
Full Path: Agricultural & Crop Insurance

Name: Federal Crop Insurance (MPCI)
Plain-English Description: Federally subsidized policies covering crop losses from natural causes like drought, flood, hail, disease and price drops.
Example: A soybean farmer buys revenue protection at 75% coverage.
US Notes: Sales closing dates and coverage levels (50%-85%) set by RMA; premium subsidies average roughly 60%.
Full Path: Agricultural & Crop Insurance > Federal Crop Insurance (MPCI)

Name: Yield Protection (YP)
Plain-English Description: Pays when harvested yield falls below a guaranteed level based on the farm's actual production history (APH).
Example: A wheat farmer's yield falls from 50 to 30 bushels per acre and the shortfall is paid.
Full Path: Agricultural & Crop Insurance > Federal Crop Insurance (MPCI) > Yield Protection (YP)

Name: Revenue Protection (RP)
Plain-English Description: Pays when revenue falls below a guarantee because of low yield, low prices or both; the guarantee rises if harvest prices go up.
Example: A corn farmer is paid when both yield and price fall.
US Notes: The most popular federal crop policy, covering the majority of insured acres.
Full Path: Agricultural & Crop Insurance > Federal Crop Insurance (MPCI) > Revenue Protection (RP)

Name: Revenue Protection with Harvest Price Exclusion (RP-HPE)
