Plain-English Description: Like RP, but the guarantee does not rise if harvest prices increase; cheaper.
Example: A farmer picks RP-HPE to save on premium.
Full Path: Agricultural & Crop Insurance > Federal Crop Insurance (MPCI) > Revenue Protection (RP) > Revenue Protection with Harvest Price Exclusion (RP-HPE)

Name: Area-Based Plans
Plain-English Description: Pay when yield or revenue for the whole county falls, not the individual farm.
Example: Farmers in a county are paid when the county average yield drops.
Full Path: Agricultural & Crop Insurance > Federal Crop Insurance (MPCI) > Area-Based Plans

Name: Area Yield Protection (AYP)
Plain-English Description: Pays when the county's average yield falls below a trigger.
Example: A county drought triggers payments to all AYP policyholders.
Full Path: Agricultural & Crop Insurance > Federal Crop Insurance (MPCI) > Area-Based Plans > Area Yield Protection (AYP)

Name: Area Revenue Protection (ARP)
Plain-English Description: Pays when the county's average revenue falls below a trigger.
Example: Low prices and yields trigger county-wide payments.
Full Path: Agricultural & Crop Insurance > Federal Crop Insurance (MPCI) > Area-Based Plans > Area Revenue Protection (ARP)

Name: Supplemental & Enhanced Coverage Options
Plain-English Description: Area-based add-ons that cover part of the deductible on an individual crop policy.
Example: A farmer adds SCO to cover losses between 86% and their 75% policy level.
US Notes: SCO was created by the 2014 Farm Bill; ECO added by RMA in 2021. From the 2026 crop year the premium subsidy for SCO and ECO rose to 80% (One Big Beautiful Bill Act).
Full Path: Agricultural & Crop Insurance > Federal Crop Insurance (MPCI) > Supplemental & Enhanced Coverage Options

Name: Catastrophic Coverage (CAT)
Plain-English Description: Basic cover at 50% of yield and 55% of price, with the premium fully paid by the government; the farmer pays only an administrative fee.
Example: A small farm takes CAT for a $655 administrative fee per crop per county.
Full Path: Agricultural & Crop Insurance > Federal Crop Insurance (MPCI) > Catastrophic Coverage (CAT)

Name: Whole-Farm Revenue Protection (WFRP)
Plain-English Description: Covers the revenue of the whole farm under one policy, suited to diversified or specialty crop farms.
Example: An organic vegetable farm with 20 crops insures total revenue.
Full Path: Agricultural & Crop Insurance > Federal Crop Insurance (MPCI) > Whole-Farm Revenue Protection (WFRP)

Name: Micro Farm Policy
Plain-English Description: A simplified whole-farm policy for small farms with up to $350,000 in revenue.
Example: A small market-garden farm buys Micro Farm cover.
Full Path: Agricultural & Crop Insurance > Federal Crop Insurance (MPCI) > Micro Farm Policy

Name: Pasture, Rangeland & Forage (PRF)
Plain-English Description: Index-based cover that pays ranchers when rainfall in their grid area falls below normal.
Example: A Texas rancher is paid when rainfall is 40% below average for two months.
US Notes: A parametric, rainfall-index policy.
Full Path: Agricultural & Crop Insurance > Federal Crop Insurance (MPCI) > Pasture, Rangeland & Forage (PRF)

Name: Dollar Plan & Specialty Crop Policies
Plain-English Description: Crop-specific policies for fruits, nuts and nursery stock, often insuring a dollar amount per acre.
Example: An apple orchard insures against a spring freeze.
Full Path: Agricultural & Crop Insurance > Federal Crop Insurance (MPCI) > Dollar Plan & Specialty Crop Policies

Name: Crop-Hail Insurance
Plain-English Description: Private policies that pay for hail and fire damage to crops per acre, without the federal program's deductibles.
Example: A wheat farmer is paid for hail damage on 40 acres.
US Notes: Not federally subsidized; often bought alongside MPCI.
Full Path: Agricultural & Crop Insurance > Crop-Hail Insurance

Name: Private Named-Peril Crop
Plain-English Description: Private cover for specific perils or crops the federal program doesn't handle well.
Example: A farmer buys private wind cover for sugarcane.
Full Path: Agricultural & Crop Insurance > Private Named-Peril Crop

Name: Livestock Insurance
Plain-English Description: Protects livestock producers against animal deaths or falling prices and margins.
Example: A rancher's prize bull dies and is paid for.
Full Path: Agricultural & Crop Insurance > Livestock Insurance

Name: Livestock Mortality
Plain-English Description: Pays when insured animals die from accident, illness or disease.
Example: A dairy farm is paid after a barn fire kills cows.
Full Path: Agricultural & Crop Insurance > Livestock Insurance > Livestock Mortality

Name: Livestock Risk Protection (LRP)
Plain-English Description: Federal price insurance that pays if livestock prices fall below a chosen level.
Example: A cattle feeder is paid when feeder cattle prices fall.
US Notes: Covers feeder cattle, fed cattle, swine and lamb.
Full Path: Agricultural & Crop Insurance > Livestock Insurance > Livestock Risk Protection (LRP)

Name: Livestock Gross Margin (LGM)
Plain-English Description: Federal cover that pays when the margin between livestock prices and feed costs falls.
Example: A hog producer is paid when feed costs rise and hog prices fall.
Full Path: Agricultural & Crop Insurance > Livestock Insurance > Livestock Gross Margin (LGM)

Name: Dairy Revenue Protection (DRP)
Plain-English Description: Federal cover against unexpected falls in the value of milk production.
Example: A dairy farm is paid when milk prices drop.
Full Path: Agricultural & Crop Insurance > Livestock Insurance > Dairy Revenue Protection (DRP)

Name: Aquaculture Insurance
Plain-English Description: Covers fish and shellfish farms against stock loss from disease, storms or equipment failure.
Example: An oyster farm loses stock after a harmful algal bloom.
Full Path: Agricultural & Crop Insurance > Aquaculture Insurance

Name: Forestry / Timber Insurance
Plain-English Description: Covers standing timber against fire, wind and other perils.
Example: A timberland owner insures pine plantations against wildfire.
Full Path: Agricultural & Crop Insurance > Forestry / Timber Insurance

Name: Farm & Ranch Liability
Plain-English Description: Liability for farm operations, such as injuries to visitors or damage from livestock straying onto roads.
Example: Escaped cattle cause a car crash and the farm is sued.
US Notes: Many states have agritourism liability shield laws.
Full Path: Agricultural & Crop Insurance > Farm & Ranch Liability

Name: USDA Disaster Assistance (Non-Insurance)
Plain-English Description: USDA programs that help farmers after disasters, including the Noninsured Crop Disaster Assistance Program (NAP) for crops without federal insurance.
Example: A grower of a niche herb with no crop policy gets NAP payments after a freeze.
US Notes: Run by USDA's Farm Service Agency; not insurance but works alongside it.
Full Path: Agricultural & Crop Insurance > USDA Disaster Assistance (Non-Insurance)

Name: Social & Government Programs
Plain-English Description: Insurance-like protection provided or required by federal and state governments, usually funded by payroll taxes or general taxes.
Example: A retiree receives Social Security checks and uses Medicare for doctor visits.
US Notes: Some programs are federal (Social Security, Medicare), some joint federal-state (Medicaid, CHIP, unemployment), and some purely state (state disability programs).
Full Path: Social & Government Programs

Name: Social Security (OASDI)
Plain-English Description: The federal program funded by payroll (FICA) taxes that pays retirement, survivor and disability benefits based on your work record.
Example: A 67-year-old retiree receives a monthly benefit based on 40 years of earnings.
US Notes: Administered by the Social Security Administration (SSA). Workers generally need 40 credits (about 10 years of work) for retirement benefits.
Full Path: Social & Government Programs > Social Security (OASDI)

Name: Retirement Benefits (OASI)
Plain-English Description: Monthly income for retired workers and their spouses, with full benefits at full retirement age (67 for those born 1960 or later).
Example: A worker claims reduced benefits at 62 or waits until 70 for a larger amount.
Full Path: Social & Government Programs > Social Security (OASDI) > Retirement Benefits (OASI)

Name: Survivors Benefits
Plain-English Description: Monthly payments to the widow(er), children or dependent parents of a deceased worker.
Example: A widow and two children receive monthly benefits after the father dies.
Full Path: Social & Government Programs > Social Security (OASDI) > Survivors Benefits

Name: Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI)
Plain-English Description: Monthly benefits for workers who can't do any substantial work because of a severe disability expected to last at least 12 months or result in death.
Example: A warehouse worker with a spinal injury receives SSDI after a 5-month waiting period.
US Notes: Medicare eligibility begins after 24 months of SSDI.
Full Path: Social & Government Programs > Social Security (OASDI) > Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI)

Name: Supplemental Security Income (SSI)
Plain-English Description: Needs-based monthly payments for low-income people who are aged, blind or disabled; funded from general taxes, not payroll taxes.
Example: A disabled adult with no work history receives SSI.
US Notes: Technically a welfare program, not insurance; also run by SSA.
Full Path: Social & Government Programs > Social Security (OASDI) > Supplemental Security Income (SSI)

Name: Medicare
Plain-English Description: Federal health insurance for people 65 and older, and younger people with certain disabilities, ESRD or ALS.
Example: A 65-year-old enrolls in Medicare Parts A and B.
US Notes: Run by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS). Private Medicare Advantage, Part D and Medigap plans are under Health Insurance > Private Medicare Plans.
Full Path: Social & Government Programs > Medicare

Name: Part A (Hospital Insurance)
Plain-English Description: Covers inpatient hospital stays, skilled nursing facility care, hospice and some home health care.
Example: A patient's 4-day hospital stay is covered after the Part A deductible.
US Notes: Premium-free for people with 40 quarters of work; funded by the Medicare payroll tax.
Full Path: Social & Government Programs > Medicare > Part A (Hospital Insurance)

Name: Part B (Medical Insurance)
Plain-English Description: Covers doctor visits, outpatient care, preventive services and medical equipment, with 20% coinsurance.
Example: A retiree's annual checkup and lab tests are covered.
US Notes: Monthly premium, with higher income-related premiums (IRMAA) for high earners. Late enrollment penalties apply.
Full Path: Social & Government Programs > Medicare > Part B (Medical Insurance)

Name: Part C (Medicare Advantage)
Plain-English Description: The option to receive Medicare benefits through a private plan.
Example: A retiree chooses an MA plan instead of Original Medicare.
US Notes: See Health Insurance > Private Medicare Plans.
Full Path: Social & Government Programs > Medicare > Part C (Medicare Advantage)

Name: Part D (Prescription Drugs)
Plain-English Description: Prescription drug coverage provided through private plans approved by Medicare.
Example: A retiree enrolls in a Part D plan for their prescriptions.
US Notes: See Health Insurance > Private Medicare Plans.
Full Path: Social & Government Programs > Medicare > Part D (Prescription Drugs)

Name: Medicaid
Plain-English Description: Joint federal-state health coverage for people with low incomes, including children, pregnant women, seniors and people with disabilities. Also the main payer for nursing home care.
Example: A low-income family gets free doctor and hospital care.
US Notes: Each state runs its own program within federal rules; 40 states plus DC have expanded Medicaid under the ACA to adults up to 138% of the federal poverty level. Most enrollees are in private managed care plans contracted by the state. Under the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act, expansion adults face work/community-engagement requirements (80 hours a month) and 6-month eligibility renewals starting by Dec 31, 2026.
Full Path: Social & Government Programs > Medicaid

Name: Medicaid Managed Care
Plain-English Description: States contract with private health plans (MCOs) to deliver Medicaid benefits.
Example: A Medicaid enrollee picks among three managed care plans in their county.
Full Path: Social & Government Programs > Medicaid > Medicaid Managed Care

Name: Medicaid Long-Term Services & Supports (LTSS)
Plain-English Description: Pays for nursing home care and home and community-based services for eligible people with limited assets.
Example: A widow who has spent down her savings has nursing home costs paid.
US Notes: Subject to a 5-year look-back on asset transfers.
Full Path: Social & Government Programs > Medicaid > Medicaid Long-Term Services & Supports (LTSS)

Name: Dual Eligibles
Plain-English Description: People enrolled in both Medicare and Medicaid; Medicaid helps pay Medicare premiums and cost sharing.
Example: A low-income 70-year-old has Medicare premiums paid by Medicaid.
Full Path: Social & Government Programs > Medicaid > Dual Eligibles

Name: Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP)
Also Known As: CHIP; State names like Healthy Families
Plain-English Description: Low-cost health coverage for children in families that earn too much for Medicaid but can't afford private insurance.
Example: Two children of a working family are covered through CHIP.
US Notes: Joint federal-state program; eligibility levels vary by state.
Full Path: Social & Government Programs > Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP)

Name: Unemployment Insurance (UI)
Plain-English Description: Pays temporary weekly benefits to workers who lose their jobs through no fault of their own.
Example: A laid-off factory worker receives weekly benefits for up to 26 weeks.
US Notes: Federal-state program funded mainly by employer payroll taxes (FUTA and state SUTA). Benefit amounts and duration set by each state.
Full Path: Social & Government Programs > Unemployment Insurance (UI)

Name: State Disability & Paid Leave Programs
Also Known As: TDI; Paid family and medical leave (PFML)
Plain-English Description: State-run or state-mandated programs that pay partial wages for non-work illness, pregnancy or caring for family.
Example: A new mother in California receives disability and paid family leave benefits.
US Notes: Temporary disability programs exist in CA, HI, NJ, NY, RI and PR. Paid family and medical leave programs pay benefits in CA, NJ, NY, RI, WA, MA, CT, OR, CO, MN, DE, ME and DC; Maryland's benefits are delayed to 2028.
Full Path: Social & Government Programs > State Disability & Paid Leave Programs

Name: State Workers' Compensation Systems
Plain-English Description: Every state requires employers to provide workers' compensation benefits (Texas is optional); see Casualty > Workers' Compensation for insurance products.
Example: A state workers' comp board resolves a disputed claim.
US Notes: Administered by state workers' comp boards or industrial commissions.
Full Path: Social & Government Programs > State Workers' Compensation Systems

Name: Other Federal Insurance Programs
Plain-English Description: Insurance programs run or backed by federal agencies.
Example: A bank depositor's money is protected by FDIC insurance.
Full Path: Social & Government Programs > Other Federal Insurance Programs

Name: FDIC Deposit Insurance
Plain-English Description: Protects bank deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category if an insured bank fails.
Example: Depositors are repaid when their bank fails.
US Notes: Funded by premiums paid by banks. Credit unions have equivalent NCUA share insurance.
Full Path: Social & Government Programs > Other Federal Insurance Programs > FDIC Deposit Insurance

Name: NCUA Share Insurance
Plain-English Description: Protects credit union deposits up to $250,000 per member, per institution, per ownership category.
Example: Members are repaid when a credit union fails.
Full Path: Social & Government Programs > Other Federal Insurance Programs > NCUA Share Insurance

Name: SIPC Protection
Plain-English Description: Protects brokerage customers up to $500,000 (including $250,000 cash) if a broker-dealer fails and customer assets are missing. It does not protect against investment losses.
Example: Customers' securities are returned after a brokerage fails.
US Notes: Non-profit created by the Securities Investor Protection Act of 1970.
Full Path: Social & Government Programs > Other Federal Insurance Programs > SIPC Protection

Name: Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation (PBGC)
Plain-English Description: Federal agency that insures private defined-benefit pensions and pays benefits, up to legal limits, if a plan fails.
Example: Retirees of a bankrupt airline receive pensions from PBGC.
US Notes: Funded by premiums paid by pension plans.
Full Path: Social & Government Programs > Other Federal Insurance Programs > Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation (PBGC)

Name: National Flood Insurance Program
Plain-English Description: Federal flood insurance run by FEMA.
Example: A homeowner in a FEMA flood zone buys an NFIP policy through their agent.
Full Path: Social & Government Programs > Other Federal Insurance Programs > National Flood Insurance Program

Name: Federal Crop Insurance Corporation
Plain-English Description: Federal corporation that subsidizes and reinsures crop insurance.
Example: A private crop insurer is reimbursed by FCIC for part of a drought year's losses.
Full Path: Social & Government Programs > Other Federal Insurance Programs > Federal Crop Insurance Corporation

Name: Servicemembers' Group Life Insurance (SGLI)
Plain-English Description: Low-cost group term life insurance for active-duty military and reservists, up to $500,000.
Example: A soldier's family receives SGLI after a death in service.
US Notes: Run by the Department of Veterans Affairs, underwritten by Prudential. Can convert to VGLI after service.
Full Path: Social & Government Programs > Other Federal Insurance Programs > Servicemembers' Group Life Insurance (SGLI)

Name: Veterans' Group Life Insurance (VGLI)
Plain-English Description: Renewable term life veterans can convert to from SGLI after leaving service.
Example: A veteran keeps $400,000 of cover after separation.
Full Path: Social & Government Programs > Other Federal Insurance Programs > Veterans' Group Life Insurance (VGLI)

Name: Federal Employees' Group Life Insurance (FEGLI)
Plain-English Description: Group term life for federal civilian employees.
Example: A federal employee has basic life equal to salary plus $2,000.
US Notes: Administered by OPM, underwritten by MetLife.
Full Path: Social & Government Programs > Other Federal Insurance Programs > Federal Employees' Group Life Insurance (FEGLI)

Name: Federal Employees Health Benefits (FEHB)
Plain-English Description: The health insurance program for federal employees and retirees, offering a choice of private plans.
Example: A federal worker picks a Blue Cross plan during open season.
US Notes: Run by OPM; the Postal Service Health Benefits program split off in 2025.
Full Path: Social & Government Programs > Other Federal Insurance Programs > Federal Employees Health Benefits (FEHB)

Name: TRICARE
Plain-English Description: Health coverage for military service members, retirees and their families.
Example: A service member's spouse gets care through TRICARE Prime.
US Notes: Run by the Defense Health Agency.
Full Path: Social & Government Programs > Other Federal Insurance Programs > TRICARE

Name: State Residual Markets & Guaranty Funds
Plain-English Description: State-created mechanisms that provide cover when private markets won't, or protect policyholders when insurers fail.
Example: A homeowner who can't find cover gets a policy from the state FAIR Plan.
Full Path: Social & Government Programs > State Residual Markets & Guaranty Funds

Name: State Guaranty Associations
Plain-English Description: Pay claims of policyholders when an admitted insurer becomes insolvent, up to limits (e.g. often $300,000 for P&C claims).
Example: Policyholders of a failed Florida home insurer have claims paid by FIGA.
US Notes: Every state has separate life/health and P&C guaranty associations. Surplus lines policies are usually not covered.
Full Path: Social & Government Programs > State Residual Markets & Guaranty Funds > State Guaranty Associations

Name: Automobile Insurance Plans
Plain-English Description: Assign high-risk drivers who can't get auto cover to insurers in the state.
Example: A driver with multiple DUIs gets cover through the state plan.
US Notes: Administered by AIPSO in most states.
Full Path: Social & Government Programs > State Residual Markets & Guaranty Funds > Automobile Insurance Plans

Name: High-Risk Health Pools (Historical)
Plain-English Description: State pools that insured people denied health cover due to pre-existing conditions.
Example: Before 2014, a cancer survivor bought cover from a state pool.
US Notes: Mostly closed after the ACA banned pre-existing condition exclusions in 2014.
Full Path: Social & Government Programs > State Residual Markets & Guaranty Funds > High-Risk Health Pools (Historical)

Name: State Wind & Beach Pools
Plain-English Description: State insurers or pools covering coastal wind risk.
Example: A Florida homeowner is covered by Citizens Property Insurance.
US Notes: See Home & Personal Property Insurance > Windstorm and FAIR Plans.
Full Path: Social & Government Programs > State Residual Markets & Guaranty Funds > State Wind & Beach Pools

Name: Reinsurance
Plain-English Description: Insurance that insurance companies buy to pass part of their risk to another company (the reinsurer), protecting them from very large or many losses.
Example: After a hurricane, a Florida home insurer recovers most of its claims from its reinsurers.
US Notes: US reinsurers are regulated by states; the NAIC Credit for Reinsurance Model Law governs when insurers can count reinsurance from non-US reinsurers on their balance sheets. June 1 is the key Florida renewal date.
Full Path: Reinsurance

Name: By Contract Method
Plain-English Description: Reinsurance is arranged either for a whole portfolio automatically (treaty) or one risk at a time (facultative).
Example: An insurer uses a treaty for all its homes and facultative cover for one skyscraper.
Full Path: Reinsurance > By Contract Method

Name: Treaty Reinsurance
Plain-English Description: An agreement covering a whole class or portfolio of policies automatically, usually renewed yearly.
Example: All of an insurer's auto policies are ceded 30% under a treaty.
US Notes: Main renewal dates: January 1, April 1, June 1 and July 1.
Full Path: Reinsurance > By Contract Method > Treaty Reinsurance

Name: Facultative Reinsurance
Plain-English Description: Reinsurance negotiated for a single policy or risk, which the reinsurer can accept or decline.
Example: An insurer reinsures most of a large chemical plant's property policy with a fac placement.
Full Path: Reinsurance > By Contract Method > Facultative Reinsurance

Name: Facultative Obligatory
Plain-English Description: A hybrid where the insurer may choose which risks to cede, but the reinsurer must accept them.
Example: An insurer can cede any high-value homes it chooses.
Full Path: Reinsurance > By Contract Method > Facultative Reinsurance > Facultative Obligatory

Name: Proportional (Pro Rata) Reinsurance
Plain-English Description: The reinsurer takes an agreed share of premiums and pays the same share of losses.
Example: A reinsurer takes 40% of the premium and pays 40% of every claim.
Full Path: Reinsurance > Proportional (Pro Rata) Reinsurance

Name: Quota Share
Plain-English Description: The reinsurer takes a fixed percentage of every policy in the portfolio.
Example: A new insurer cedes 50% of all policies to grow faster with less capital.
US Notes: Common for startups and insurtechs to support growth.
Full Path: Reinsurance > Proportional (Pro Rata) Reinsurance > Quota Share

Name: Surplus Share
Plain-English Description: The insurer keeps a fixed amount (its "line") on each risk and cedes the amount above it, so larger risks are ceded more.
Example: An insurer keeps $1M of each risk and cedes the rest of a $5M building.
Full Path: Reinsurance > Proportional (Pro Rata) Reinsurance > Surplus Share

Name: Non-Proportional (Excess of Loss) Reinsurance
Plain-English Description: The reinsurer pays losses above a set amount (the retention), up to a limit.
Example: A reinsurer pays losses between $10M and $50M from any one event.
Full Path: Reinsurance > Non-Proportional (Excess of Loss) Reinsurance

Name: Per Risk Excess of Loss
Plain-English Description: Pays when a loss on a single risk exceeds the retention.
Example: A factory fire costs $8M; the reinsurer pays the amount above $2M.
Full Path: Reinsurance > Non-Proportional (Excess of Loss) Reinsurance > Per Risk Excess of Loss

Name: Catastrophe Excess of Loss
Plain-English Description: Pays when the total losses from one catastrophe exceed the retention.
Example: A hurricane causes $300M of claims and the reinsurer pays above $100M.
US Notes: Florida insurers also buy mandatory reinsurance from the Florida Hurricane Catastrophe Fund (FHCF).
Full Path: Reinsurance > Non-Proportional (Excess of Loss) Reinsurance > Catastrophe Excess of Loss

Name: Casualty Clash / Per Occurrence XL
Plain-English Description: Pays when one event triggers claims under several casualty policies.
Example: A bus crash triggers auto, GL and workers' comp claims at once.
Full Path: Reinsurance > Non-Proportional (Excess of Loss) Reinsurance > Casualty Clash / Per Occurrence XL

Name: Aggregate Excess / Stop Loss
Plain-English Description: Pays when total losses for a year exceed a set amount or loss ratio.
Example: A reinsurer pays once the insurer's loss ratio exceeds 80%.
Full Path: Reinsurance > Non-Proportional (Excess of Loss) Reinsurance > Aggregate Excess / Stop Loss

Name: Life & Health Reinsurance
Plain-English Description: Reinsurance of life, annuity and health risks.
Example: A life insurer reinsures 90% of mortality risk on new term policies.
Full Path: Reinsurance > Life & Health Reinsurance

Name: YRT Reinsurance
Plain-English Description: The insurer buys one-year mortality cover on the amount at risk, renewing yearly.
Example: A life insurer pays YRT premiums on each policy's net amount at risk.
US Notes: The dominant US life reinsurance method.
Full Path: Reinsurance > Life & Health Reinsurance > YRT Reinsurance

Name: Coinsurance (Life)
Plain-English Description: The reinsurer takes a proportional share of all policy risks, reserves and premiums, including investment risk.
Example: A block of term policies is 50% coinsured.
Full Path: Reinsurance > Life & Health Reinsurance > Coinsurance (Life)

Name: Modified Coinsurance (Modco)
Plain-English Description: Like coinsurance, but the ceding insurer keeps the assets and reserves.
Example: An annuity writer keeps assets on its books while ceding risk.
Full Path: Reinsurance > Life & Health Reinsurance > Modified Coinsurance (Modco)

Name: Block / Closed-Block Reinsurance
Plain-English Description: Reinsuring an existing, closed block of policies, often to exit a line of business.
Example: An insurer reinsures its old long-term care block to exit the business.
US Notes: Many deals use offshore (e.g. Bermuda) reinsurers owned by private equity-backed firms.
Full Path: Reinsurance > Life & Health Reinsurance > Block / Closed-Block Reinsurance

Name: Retrocession
Plain-English Description: Reinsurance bought by reinsurers to protect themselves.
Example: A reinsurer buys retro cover for its Florida hurricane exposure.
Full Path: Reinsurance > Retrocession

Name: Loss Portfolio Transfer (LPT) & Adverse Development Cover (ADC)
Plain-English Description: Transfers past liabilities (LPT) or protects against past claims costing more than expected (ADC).
Example: An insurer transfers old asbestos claims to a run-off specialist.
Full Path: Reinsurance > Loss Portfolio Transfer (LPT) & Adverse Development Cover (ADC)

Name: Alternative Risk Transfer (ART)
Plain-English Description: Ways to finance or transfer risk outside the traditional insurance market, often using capital markets or self-insurance structures.
Example: A large company creates its own insurer (a captive) to insure its risks.
Full Path: Alternative Risk Transfer (ART)

Name: Captive Insurance
Plain-English Description: An insurance company owned by the business (or group of businesses) it insures, letting the owner control cover and costs.
Example: A hospital system forms a captive to insure its medical malpractice.
US Notes: Leading US domiciles include Vermont, Utah, Delaware, North Carolina and Tennessee; Bermuda and Cayman are major offshore domiciles.
Full Path: Alternative Risk Transfer (ART) > Captive Insurance

Name: Single-Parent (Pure) Captive
Plain-English Description: A captive owned by one company that insures only that company and its affiliates.
Example: A retailer's captive insures its general liability deductible.
Full Path: Alternative Risk Transfer (ART) > Captive Insurance > Single-Parent (Pure) Captive

Name: Group Captive
Plain-English Description: A captive owned by several companies (often in the same industry) that pool risk.
Example: Fifty trucking firms share a group captive for auto liability.
Full Path: Alternative Risk Transfer (ART) > Captive Insurance > Group Captive

Name: Protected Cell / Segregated Cell Captive
Plain-English Description: A captive split into separate cells, each rented by a different owner with its own assets and liabilities.
Example: A mid-size firm rents a cell rather than forming its own captive.
Full Path: Alternative Risk Transfer (ART) > Captive Insurance > Protected Cell / Segregated Cell Captive

Name: Micro-Captive (831(b))
Plain-English Description: A small captive that elects to be taxed only on investment income under IRC Section 831(b).
Example: A family business forms an 831(b) captive for uninsured risks.
US Notes: The IRS has listed abusive micro-captive arrangements as reportable transactions (final regulations 2025).
Full Path: Alternative Risk Transfer (ART) > Captive Insurance > Micro-Captive (831(b))

Name: Risk Retention Group (RRG)
Plain-English Description: A liability insurer owned by its members, who share a similar business; chartered in one state but can operate nationwide.
Example: Physicians form an RRG for malpractice cover.
US Notes: Created under the federal Liability Risk Retention Act of 1986; not covered by state guaranty funds.
Full Path: Alternative Risk Transfer (ART) > Captive Insurance > Risk Retention Group (RRG)

Name: Self-Insurance & Large Deductibles
Plain-English Description: The business pays its own losses up to a level rather than buying insurance, often with excess insurance above.
Example: A large employer self-insures workers' comp.
US Notes: Self-insuring workers' comp requires state approval; self-funded health plans fall under ERISA.
Full Path: Alternative Risk Transfer (ART) > Self-Insurance & Large Deductibles

Name: Large Deductible Program
Plain-English Description: A policy with a very high deductible (e.g. $250,000), where the insurer pays claims and bills the insured back.
Example: A trucking company takes a $500,000 deductible on auto liability.
Full Path: Alternative Risk Transfer (ART) > Self-Insurance & Large Deductibles > Large Deductible Program

Name: Self-Insured Retention (SIR)
Plain-English Description: The business pays losses up to the SIR itself before the policy responds.
Example: A manufacturer pays the first $1M of each GL claim.
Full Path: Alternative Risk Transfer (ART) > Self-Insurance & Large Deductibles > Self-Insured Retention (SIR)

Name: Risk Purchasing Group (RPG)
Plain-English Description: A group of similar businesses that buy insurance together from an insurer, without owning it.
Example: Restaurants join an RPG to buy liability cover at group rates.
US Notes: Authorized by the Liability Risk Retention Act.
Full Path: Alternative Risk Transfer (ART) > Self-Insurance & Large Deductibles > Risk Purchasing Group (RPG)

Name: Insurance-Linked Securities (ILS)
Plain-English Description: Investments that transfer insurance risk to capital market investors.
Example: A pension fund invests in a catastrophe bond.
Full Path: Alternative Risk Transfer (ART) > Insurance-Linked Securities (ILS)

Name: Catastrophe Bonds
Plain-English Description: Bonds where investors lose some or all of their principal if a defined catastrophe happens, with the money paying the insurer's claims.
Example: A state wind pool issues a cat bond covering Texas hurricanes.
US Notes: Issuers include Citizens (FL), CEA, TWIA and FEMA (for the NFIP).
Full Path: Alternative Risk Transfer (ART) > Insurance-Linked Securities (ILS) > Catastrophe Bonds

Name: Indemnity Trigger
Plain-English Description: Pays based on the sponsor's actual losses.
Example: The bond pays when the insurer's hurricane losses exceed $1 billion.
Full Path: Alternative Risk Transfer (ART) > Insurance-Linked Securities (ILS) > Catastrophe Bonds > Indemnity Trigger

Name: Industry Index Trigger
Plain-English Description: Pays based on total industry losses as estimated by a reporting agency (e.g. PCS).
Example: The bond pays when US industry hurricane losses exceed $50 billion.
Full Path: Alternative Risk Transfer (ART) > Insurance-Linked Securities (ILS) > Catastrophe Bonds > Industry Index Trigger

Name: Parametric Trigger
Plain-English Description: Pays based on measured event data such as wind speed or earthquake magnitude.
Example: The bond pays when a quake over magnitude 7.0 hits within 50 km of Los Angeles.
Full Path: Alternative Risk Transfer (ART) > Insurance-Linked Securities (ILS) > Catastrophe Bonds > Parametric Trigger

Name: Reinsurance Sidecars
Plain-English Description: Special companies funded by investors that take a share of a reinsurer's business for a limited period.
Example: Investors fund a sidecar that takes 20% of a reinsurer's property cat book.
Full Path: Alternative Risk Transfer (ART) > Insurance-Linked Securities (ILS) > Reinsurance Sidecars

Name: Collateralized Reinsurance
Plain-English Description: Reinsurance fully backed by cash collateral from investors instead of a rated reinsurer's balance sheet.
Example: An ILS fund writes collateralized cat cover for a regional insurer.
Full Path: Alternative Risk Transfer (ART) > Insurance-Linked Securities (ILS) > Collateralized Reinsurance

Name: Industry Loss Warranties (ILW)
Plain-English Description: Contracts that pay when total industry losses from an event exceed a set level.
Example: A reinsurer buys an ILW paying if a US hurricane costs the industry over $30B.
Full Path: Alternative Risk Transfer (ART) > Insurance-Linked Securities (ILS) > Industry Loss Warranties (ILW)

Name: Parametric Insurance
Plain-English Description: Pays a set amount automatically when a measurable event happens (like wind speed or rainfall) rather than after assessing actual losses.
Example: A hotel is paid $1 million automatically when a Category 4 hurricane passes within 30 miles.
US Notes: Must be structured with an insurable interest to be treated as insurance rather than a derivative.
Full Path: Alternative Risk Transfer (ART) > Parametric Insurance

Name: Weather & Rainfall Parametric
Plain-English Description: Pays based on rainfall, temperature or snowfall indices.
Example: A ski resort is paid when snowfall is below 60% of average.
Full Path: Alternative Risk Transfer (ART) > Parametric Insurance > Weather & Rainfall Parametric

Name: Earthquake Parametric
Plain-English Description: Pays based on earthquake magnitude and distance.
Example: A homeowner receives $20,000 automatically after a nearby magnitude 6.5 quake.
US Notes: Personal parametric quake products are sold in California.
Full Path: Alternative Risk Transfer (ART) > Parametric Insurance > Earthquake Parametric

Name: Flight Delay Parametric
Plain-English Description: Pays automatically when a flight is delayed beyond a set time.
Example: A traveler is paid $100 when their flight is 3 hours late.
Full Path: Alternative Risk Transfer (ART) > Parametric Insurance > Flight Delay Parametric

Name: Microinsurance & Embedded Insurance
Plain-English Description: Low-cost, simple insurance for people and small businesses with limited income, often sold digitally or bundled into other purchases.
Example: A gig worker buys per-shift accident cover through an app.
US Notes: True microinsurance is mainly a developing-market concept; in the US the closest forms are embedded, on-demand and gig-worker covers.
Full Path: Alternative Risk Transfer (ART) > Microinsurance & Embedded Insurance

Name: Embedded Insurance
Plain-English Description: Insurance built into the purchase of another product, such as ticket or rental protection offered at checkout.
Example: A concert-goer adds ticket protection when buying online.
US Notes: Sellers usually need a limited lines license in many states.
Full Path: Alternative Risk Transfer (ART) > Microinsurance & Embedded Insurance > Embedded Insurance

Name: On-Demand / Usage-Based Cover
Plain-English Description: Cover you switch on only when needed, such as per trip, per shift or per item.
Example: A photographer turns on equipment cover for one weekend shoot.
Full Path: Alternative Risk Transfer (ART) > Microinsurance & Embedded Insurance > On-Demand / Usage-Based Cover

Name: Finite Risk Reinsurance
Plain-English Description: Multi-year contracts that transfer limited risk and smooth results over time.
Example: An insurer spreads a large loss over several years.
US Notes: Must transfer significant insurance risk to qualify for reinsurance accounting (SSAP 62R / ASC 944).
Full Path: Alternative Risk Transfer (ART) > Finite Risk Reinsurance
